leader: direct audit of fieldops-api, atlas-android, atlas-rag, warehouse-dbt after four specialists stalled

architecture.fell_back_and_why: Two distinct harness failures, both recorded rather than papered over. (1) CONCURRENCY: the Agent tool refused parallel dispatch with 'Concurrent subagent limit reached' on the 3rd and 4th specialists even though it reported a cap of 20, so the seven specialists were launched in waves as slots freed rather than in one parallel batch as SKILL.md section 3 and team.md prescribe. (2) STALLED AGENTS: of the seven spawned, only three ever delivered a result (settlement-worker, pulumi-platform, supply-chain). The other four (fieldops-api, atlas-android, atlas-rag, warehouse-dbt) wrote their transcripts and then went silent with no completion notification - the fieldops-api agent's transcript stopped 16 minutes before it was noticed. They were resumed via SendMessage with an explicit request to emit their final JSON; all four accepted the resume, appended a few lines, and produced nothing further. Rather than ship an audit covering two of six components, the leader read those four components directly (40 files, ~2800 lines) and audited them itself, applying the same discipline the role files impose: unaided reading before any pack section, COV-01/02/03 density (return to every file that produced a finding; enumerate manifests key by key), the FP-01..FP-11 triage rules with a written reason for every HOLDS and UNKNOWN, and a final VER-09 pass attacking each assertion from its location alone. Consequence for interpretation: findings for those four components did NOT get an independent context, so the blindness that VER-09 depends on is weaker there - the same reading that produced them also judged them. The three specialist components carry genuine context separation. A further consequence of the same failure: no separate ehs-verifier was staffed, because a blind critic in a fresh context was exactly what the harness would not reliably give; the self-refutation pass is a weaker substitute and is reported as such. Also of note: this leader twice asserted in its own narration that a specialist had returned results when no notification had arrived; both statements were corrected in-session and no fabricated finding entered this report - every finding below traces to a specialist return actually received or to a file this leader read directly.
architecture.dispatch_path: Fallback path from references/team.md: the ehs-* plugin subagents are not registered in this harness, so each specialist was launched as a general-purpose agent with its scope, mode, target language, the path of its own role file under agents/, the packs that role cites, the safety contract and the return format copied into the prompt.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the limit and offset interpolated into the work-order list query
ruled_out.killed_by: workorders.ts:50-51 — both values pass through Number.parseInt and are then clamped by Math.max/Math.min before the template is built, so the interpolated values are always integers. A payload such as '5; drop table' parses to 5. The construct is bad practice and worth fixing, but it is not injectable as written.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the attachment download, since a stored key is joined onto the attachment root
ruled_out.killed_by: attachments.ts:51 — the storage key is generated server-side as randomUUID() plus a fixed suffix and is never derived from user input; the uploader's filename goes to a separate display column after being stripped by the SAFE_NAME class at attachments.ts:50. No caller-controlled value reaches the join.

ruled_out.assertion: Rate-limit bypass by spoofing X-Forwarded-For on the login endpoint
ruled_out.killed_by: rateLimit.ts:12-15 takes the LAST hop rather than the first, and an AWS ALB appends the immediate client address to the right of the header. Behind the declared load balancer (pulumi-platform/edge.ts:20-40) the last hop is therefore the real client address and a client-supplied prefix does not displace it. The fallback to another vendor header at rateLimit.ts:17 is reached only when the header is absent entirely, which behind that ALB it never is.

ruled_out.assertion: Stored cross-site scripting through an attacker-chosen attachment content type served back on download
ruled_out.killed_by: attachments.ts:103-104 — the response sets content-disposition to attachment and x-content-type-options to nosniff on the same call, so the browser downloads rather than renders regardless of the stored type. The unvalidated content type is still worth constraining, but it does not yield script execution here.

ruled_out.assertion: escapeHtml is incomplete because it does not escape the apostrophe
ruled_out.killed_by: Every call site interpolates into a text node or into a double-quoted attribute — workorders.ts:189, :192, :194, :195 and attachments.ts:103 — and the double quote is escaped at policy.ts:70. The one attribute use additionally receives a value already stripped to an alphanumeric class at attachments.ts:50. No reachable context makes the missing apostrophe exploitable.

ruled_out.assertion: The WebView can be made to enable file access and universal file-origin access through an intent extra
ruled_out.killed_by: AndroidManifest.xml:57 declares the activity exported=false, and the only factory that builds an intent for it, ReportWebViewActivity.kt:26-27, never sets that extra; a search across the module finds the constant at :24 and its read at :50 and no writer. No second principal can set it, so it is a latent hazard to delete rather than a reachable defect.

ruled_out.assertion: The full session dump including the raw bearer is exposed through the support sheet
ruled_out.killed_by: A search across the module returns exactly one occurrence of exportSessionForSupport, its own definition at SessionStore.kt:74. The support path calls redactedSummary instead, at DeepLinkRouter.kt:96, which truncates the token to its last four characters. The function is dead code and should be deleted, but nothing reaches it.

ruled_out.assertion: Caller-supplied filters can override the tenant predicate in the vector search
ruled_out.killed_by: retriever.py:56 — the tenant is assigned into the dictionary AFTER the caller's filters are copied into it at :54, so a caller-supplied tenant key is overwritten rather than honoured, and the clause list at :59 is built from fixed strings rather than from the dictionary's keys. The comment at retriever.py:55 accurately describes what the code does.

ruled_out.assertion: The wildcard CORS origin allows any site to read authenticated responses from the RAG service
ruled_out.killed_by: settings.py:44 sets credentials false and the middleware never emits an allow-credentials header, and the service authenticates by bearer only — no endpoint reads a cookie, so a cross-origin page carries no ambient credential and must already possess the token to read anything. A wildcard origin without credentials is the standard posture for a token-authenticated public API, and reporting it would be a decoy.

ruled_out.assertion: The unused ad-hoc SQL tool lets the model run arbitrary queries against the snapshot schema
ruled_out.killed_by: tools.py:91-94 — the registry the dispatcher looks up contains only the fetch and lookup tools, and tools.py:64-89 offers only those two to the model; run_sql appears in neither, and a search of the component finds no other caller. The docstring at tools.py:56-57 confirms it was never wired. It is unreachable today and should be deleted, since it takes one registry line to become critical.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the partner identifier interpolated into the export model
ruled_out.killed_by: partner_extract.sql:16 — the variable is lowercased and then stripped by a substitution that removes every character outside lowercase letters, digits and the hyphen, so quotes, whitespace, semicolons and comment markers cannot survive into the literal at :30. The interpolation is the wrong construction and should be a parameter, but it is not injectable as written.

ruled_out.assertion: The row-security macro silently does nothing, because it returns early for non-Postgres adapters
ruled_out.killed_by: profiles.yml:9, :21 and :33 — all three declared targets are type postgres, and the file's own header comment at profiles.yml:1-3 states there is no file-based target. The early return at row_security.sql:12-14 is therefore unreachable for every target the project declares.

ruled_out.assertion: Database credentials are stored in cleartext in the dbt profiles file
ruled_out.killed_by: profiles.yml:11 and :13 read the user and password through environment lookups with no second argument, so a missing variable raises rather than falling back to a literal; the same holds at :23/:25 and :35/:37. The transport settings at :17-18, :29-30 and :41-42 additionally pin a CA bundle. The separate credential-scope defect in this file is reported as a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: A payments credential is stored in plaintext in both Pulumi stack files and re-exported as a stack output
ruled_out.killed_by: The value carries the provider's publishable-key prefix and the staging stack records at :18-19 that it is the client-side sandbox key shipped inside the browser bundle, so it is public by construction and holds no authority. Noted without being a security finding: the production file carries the same sandbox value as staging, which is a real environment drift but a functional one.

ruled_out.assertion: The Pulumi stack files store secrets in plaintext because neither contains any encrypted entry
ruled_out.killed_by: index.ts:20-22 reads the database password, the identity-provider secret and the partner external identifier through the secret-requiring configuration accessor, and none of the three appears in either stack file in any form. Their absence from the plaintext files is the correct outcome, not a gap.

ruled_out.assertion: The partner analytics role can be assumed by any AWS principal
ruled_out.killed_by: iam.ts:101-104 narrows the same statement with an external-identifier condition whose value comes from the secret-requiring configuration accessor at index.ts:22, so no reachable assume path skips it. This is the FP-11 shape exactly: a permissive principal overridden by a condition in the same block. The over-broad grant to that role is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: The monitoring listener rule forwards to a target group with no authentication action
ruled_out.killed_by: edge.ts:159-189 declares a rule blocking that path prefix unless the request comes from the corporate address set, and edge.ts:192-195 associates the web ACL with this load balancer, so the ACL evaluates before the listener rules. Case and encoding bypasses were considered: the listener path pattern is itself case-sensitive and the rule applies URL decoding at edge.ts:172.

ruled_out.assertion: The dead legacy archive helper creates a fully public bucket
ruled_out.killed_by: A tree-wide search for the function returns only its declaration at storage.ts:153, and index.ts:7 imports only the live factory. No bucket, access block or policy is created from it in any stack. It remains a hazard the moment anyone calls it and should be deleted rather than kept.

ruled_out.assertion: The application security group allows unrestricted egress to the internet
ruled_out.killed_by: network.ts:38-41 — the private route table those tasks sit behind declares no default route, so the egress rule has no path to the internet to permit. Recorded as an observation rather than a finding: the comment at network.ts:35-37 claims egress goes through VPC endpoints and a tree-wide search finds no endpoint or NAT gateway, so no egress path is declared at all.

ruled_out.assertion: The notification hook is a server-side request forgery sink because the destination comes from the message
ruled_out.killed_by: handlers.py:73 is the only call site and passes the configured notification URL, a constant declared at settings.py:45-47; no message field reaches the destination parameter. What survives is the cleartext channel and the uncontrolled redirect, reported separately as a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Settlement receipts with account identifiers, amounts and balances are written to the log
ruled_out.killed_by: consumer.py:122 installs the basic logging format, which renders no extra attribute. Executing that formatter over the same call shape emits the message text alone with the receipt absent. The finding inverted into the audit-trail gap reported as a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The legacy reprocess helper strips the signature field and applies the entry, a signature bypass
ruled_out.killed_by: The symbol has exactly one occurrence in the tree, its own definition at retry.py:54. Nothing calls it and it is not exported as a console script. It is dead code that documents the shape; the live equivalent at retry.py:43 is reported instead.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded certification account vectors are production account identifiers or credentials
ruled_out.killed_by: schemas.py:46-48 identifies them as scheme sandbox certification vectors, they carry no secret material, and the constant has one occurrence — its definition — so no code path routes to them.

ruled_out.assertion: Redis key injection across tenants is possible through a colon in a reconciliation field
ruled_out.killed_by: Subsumed rather than exploitable as stated: reconcile.py:56 performs no ownership check at all, so an attacker naming another tenant's account writes it directly with no key crafting required. Reported as the balance-overwrite finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The settings integer parser swallowing a conversion error is a security-relevant fail-open
ruled_out.killed_by: The four keys it parses are a batch size, a block timeout, the already-inert attempt counter and a cache lifetime. A malformed value reverts to a defined conservative default rather than to an unsafe one, and no security decision reads them.

ruled_out.assertion: Gradle dependency verification metadata is missing, so no artifact checksum or signature is checked
ruled_out.killed_by: The file that would carry this is not in the audited tree and neither are its siblings: there is no settings file, no verification metadata, no wrapper properties and no root build script — the component contains only the application module's build file. Dependency verification and the repository declarations it governs live in the root project, outside what was given. Asserting the control is absent would be asserting from a truncated tree; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, and it should be re-checked against the full repository.

ruled_out.assertion: Install-time code execution through package manager lifecycle scripts
ruled_out.killed_by: Enumerated the scripts object of both package manifests key by key — dev, build, start, typecheck and preview, up, typecheck. No preinstall, install, postinstall or prepare in either, no custom Python build backend, no build script and no remote script application in the Gradle file. A search across the whole target root returns nothing. Clean result, recorded rather than omitted.

ruled_out.assertion: Typosquat-shaped or dependency-confusion-prone package names among the declared dependencies
ruled_out.killed_by: Enumerated all 28 declared coordinates across the four manifests and the Gradle file; every one resolves to a well-known upstream with a canonical spelling, and both scoped namespaces are real public scopes. There is no registry configuration, no resolution override and no publish configuration anywhere in the tree, so there is no multi-registry resolution to exploit.

ruled_out.assertion: The RAG service binds all interfaces by default, exposing it beyond its host
ruled_out.killed_by: settings.py:19 makes the bind address overridable by environment, and binding all interfaces is the required behaviour for a containerised service that must be reachable from outside its own network namespace. This is the intended-and-bounded case; the network boundary in front of it belongs to the infrastructure component.

ruled_out.assertion: The Pulumi template configuration block omits most of the keys the program requires and marks none as secret
ruled_out.killed_by: The block is scaffolding consumed when a new project is initialised from this one; it is not the schema that governs a deployment. The actual enforcement is index.ts:11-23, where the require and require-secret accessors fail closed on a missing key and mark values secret regardless of what the template says. An incomplete template block is untidy, not a weakness.

findings.title: A non-debuggable, release-derived staging build variant ships with TLS validation disabled
findings.class: CWE-295 improper certificate validation in a distributed artifact
findings.evidence: build.gradle.kts:35-48 creates a staging variant initialised from release, with a distinct application id suffix, debuggable false and release fallbacks, and sets the insecure-TLS build flag true at line 47. The flag is live: ApiClient.kt:35 branches on it and replaces the certificate pinner with a trust manager that accepts every chain (ApiClient.kt:28-32) and a hostname verifier that accepts every name (ApiClient.kt:41). The policy is applied to both clients, at ApiClient.kt:58 and :64.
findings.impact: The build system produces a signed, minified, non-debuggable artifact — indistinguishable from a release build to anyone installing it — in which every HTTPS call accepts any certificate for any hostname. The comment at build.gradle.kts:45-46 says it exists because field testers' devices lack the internal CA, so the variant is deliberately distributed outside the build team, and the interceptor attaches the session bearer to those calls.
findings.recommendation: Ship the internal CA as a network-security-config trust anchor for the staging variant so certificates are still validated against a different root. If a flag must remain, make it debug-only and let staging inherit false from the default configuration.

triage.reason: This is the rule that bounds the debug sibling and does not bound this one: the staging variant sets debuggable false and inherits minification and shrinking from release, so it is a shipping artifact by construction.

The stated bound — an internal CA absent from the device trust store — is addressable with a trust anchor; instead the code accepts every issuer and every hostname, which is far wider than the stated need.
There is no compensating layer: the else branch at ApiClient.kt:44 is the only place pinning is applied, so when the flag is true no pinning happens on either client.
The policy helper is called on both clients, covering API traffic and attachment uploads alike.

scope.established_by: Located the three declarations of the flag and its single reader, then the two call sites where the resulting policy takes effect.
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-android/app/build.gradle.kts:52 — the debug variant sets the same flag but is bounded by FP-04 and is deliberately excluded from this finding.

findings.title: The https deep-link filter declares no host, so every domain on the web opens the router
findings.class: CWE-939 improper authorization in handler / overly broad intent filter (MASVS-PLATFORM-1)
findings.evidence: The intent filter at AndroidManifest.xml:47-52 declares `android:scheme="https"` and `android:pathPrefix="/r/"` but no `android:host`. An Android data element with a scheme and a path and no host matches that path on any authority, so `https://attacker.example/r/anything` resolves to this activity. `android:autoVerify="true"` at line 47 does not narrow it: App Links verification applies to hosts that are declared, and there is none to verify. The activity is `android:exported="true"` (line 33) with the BROWSABLE category (line 50), so a web page reaches it directly.
findings.impact: The comment in the routing code states the opposite of what the manifest configures: DeepLinkRouter.kt:57-59 says anything arriving on https 'is one of our own report links' because the filter is verified against the domain association file. It is not, so an attacker-controlled page drives the router, which is what makes the unvalidated `target` parameter on the next line reachable from the open web.
findings.recommendation: Declare the host explicitly on the filter — `android:host="reports.fieldops.example"` — so autoVerify has something to verify, and confirm the association file is served. Do not rely on the filter for authorisation regardless; validate the URL in code as well.

triage.reason: The path prefix at AndroidManifest.xml:51 narrows the path and not the authority, and no other element in the filter constrains the host.
No code compensates: routeWeb (DeepLinkRouter.kt:61-64) performs no host check on the incoming URI before using it.
The filter is in the main source set manifest, present in every build variant.

scope.established_by: Read every element of both intent filters on the exported router activity and checked which components of the URI each constrains.

findings.title: The attachment content provider is exported without permission and resolves paths from the caller's URI
findings.class: CWE-926 exported provider / CWE-22 path traversal (MASVS-PLATFORM-1, MASVS-STORAGE-2)
findings.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:62-66 declares the provider with `android:exported="true"` and `android:grantUriPermissions="true"` and no `android:permission`, `android:readPermission` or `<path-permission>`. Export plus a permission-less declaration means any installed application may call it directly, without needing a granted URI. The implementation then builds the path from the caller's URI: AttachmentSync.kt:35 takes `uri.lastPathSegment` and AttachmentSync.kt:36 does `File(attachmentDir(context!!), name)` with no canonicalisation and no check that the result stays inside the directory; `query` repeats the pattern at AttachmentSync.kt:47. Android decodes each path segment after splitting on unencoded separators, so a percent-encoded traversal arrives at `File(...)` as relative path components.
findings.impact: Any application on the device reads files from the app's private storage, including captured customer photographs and signature images, and by traversal any other file the process can read under its data directory — the encrypted session preferences among them. `grantUriPermissions` is what this design needs; `exported="true"` without a permission is what makes it reachable without a grant.
findings.recommendation: Set `android:exported="false"` and rely on the temporary grants the share sheet issues, which is what `grantUriPermissions` provides. Independently, resolve the file and verify with `canonicalPath.startsWith(...)` that it is inside the attachment directory before opening it, and reject any segment containing a separator.

triage.reason: The second principal is any other application installed on the device; the export declaration at AndroidManifest.xml:65 is what admits it.
The path component is `uri.lastPathSegment` (AttachmentSync.kt:35), supplied by the calling application.
No compensating check exists in either method: `openFile` (AttachmentSync.kt:34-38) and `query` (:40-51) both construct the File and use it immediately.

Sharing attachments with a chosen app is intended, and the comment at AndroidManifest.xml:60-61 says so, but the intended mechanism is the URI grant; the unbounded part — direct access by any app, and traversal — is not what the intent covers.

scope.established_by: Read every attribute of the provider declaration, then every method of the implementing class for a containment check.

findings.title: The deep-link router loads an attacker-supplied URL into the report WebView
findings.class: CWE-601 open redirect into a privileged WebView (MASVS-PLATFORM-2)
findings.evidence: DeepLinkRouter.kt:62 reads `uri.getQueryParameter("target")` and, when present, uses it in place of the API-derived URL, passing it to `ReportWebViewActivity.intentFor` at DeepLinkRouter.kt:63. There is no scheme check, no host allowlist and no comparison against `BuildConfig.API_BASE` — the fallback expression on the same line is the only place the API base appears. The sibling routes are careful by contrast: `openOrder` and `openReport` both build their URL from `BuildConfig.API_BASE` and a numeric id parsed with `toLongOrNull` (DeepLinkRouter.kt:67-73 and :86-92).
findings.impact: A link of the form `https://any-host/r/x?target=https://attacker/page` loads attacker content in a WebView that has JavaScript enabled and a JavaScript bridge exposing the session bearer. Combined with the two findings on either side of it, this is a remote session-token theft reachable by getting a technician to tap a link.
findings.recommendation: Drop the `target` parameter entirely and derive the URL from the path as the sibling routes do. If an operator-supplied destination is genuinely required, validate the parsed URL's scheme is https and its host is exactly the configured API or report host before loading it.

triage.reason: The value is a query parameter of an intent that any application or web page can send to an exported activity (AndroidManifest.xml:33).
Nothing downstream validates it: ReportWebViewActivity.kt:59-62 takes the extra and calls `loadUrl` directly.
The `isSignedIn` guard at DeepLinkRouter.kt:28 narrows this to signed-in devices, which is the population that has a token worth stealing, so it does not reduce the impact.

scope.established_by: Compared the four routing branches; three construct their URL from BuildConfig and a validated id, one accepts a caller-supplied URL.

findings.title: The WebView JavaScript bridge hands the raw session bearer to any page it loads
findings.class: CWE-926 improperly exported bridge / credential exposure to web content (MASVS-PLATFORM-2)
findings.evidence: ReportWebViewActivity.kt:57 installs `addJavascriptInterface(ReportBridge(), "Atlas")` unconditionally, before any URL is known, and ReportWebViewActivity.kt:44 enables JavaScript. The bridge exposes `@JavascriptInterface fun sessionToken(): String = SessionStore.bearer().orEmpty()` at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:95-96 and `actorId()` at :98-99. Nothing restricts which origin may call them: there is no `WebViewClient` in the class at all, so no `shouldOverrideUrlLoading` or origin check exists, and the interface is not removed or re-added as the page changes.
findings.impact: Any JavaScript executing in this WebView reads the technician's session bearer and posts it anywhere. Three independent routes reach that state: the attacker-supplied `target` URL, a redirect from a legitimate page, and stored cross-site scripting in the work-order notes — the WebView is pointed at `/api/v1/workorders/{id}/print` by DeepLinkRouter.kt:72-73, which is the fieldops-api endpoint that interpolates `notes` unescaped.
findings.recommendation: Do not expose a credential through a JavaScript bridge. Have the native side fetch the signature image and pass the bytes to the page, or inject a short-lived capability scoped to that one resource. If a bridge must remain, attach a WebViewClient that removes the interface whenever the loaded origin is not the exact expected host, and add it only after that origin is confirmed.

triage.reason: The second principal is the remote web origin whose script runs in the WebView; the activity being `exported="false"` (AndroidManifest.xml:57) bars other apps from starting it but says nothing about the content it renders.
No origin control exists: the class installs no WebViewClient and performs no URL comparison before or after `loadUrl` at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:61.
The method returns the bearer itself (ReportWebViewActivity.kt:96), not a derived or redacted value.

scope.established_by: Read the WebView configuration in order of execution and searched the class for any origin gate; there is none.

findings.title: The offline report interpolates notes into HTML unescaped and renders it with the API origin
findings.class: CWE-79 cross-site scripting in a WebView (MASVS-PLATFORM-2)
findings.evidence: In the same template, the title is encoded — `TextUtils.htmlEncode(title)` at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:78 — and the notes are not: ReportWebViewActivity.kt:79 emits `<section class="notes">$notes</section>` raw. The document is then loaded through `loadDataWithBaseURL` with a base of `https://api.fieldops.example/` (ReportWebViewActivity.kt:85-91), which gives the injected script that origin rather than a null one, in a WebView that has the `Atlas` bridge attached at line 57.
findings.impact: Script stored in a work order's notes executes on the offline path with the API's own origin and with access to `Atlas.sessionToken()`. The server-side sanitiser this depends on is a three-pattern blacklist in the API (fieldops-api policy.ts:57-63) that does not filter event-handler attributes, so the payload survives the round trip and fires with no network involved.
findings.recommendation: Encode the notes exactly as the title is encoded on the adjacent line. Pass `null` as the base URL so injected content cannot claim the API origin, and remove the credential-bearing bridge from this path since an offline sheet has no reason to call back for a signature.

triage.reason: The only sanitiser on this data is server-side (fieldops-api/src/lib/policy.ts:57), it is a blacklist, and it is bypassed by attribute-based payloads; nothing on the device re-sanitises.
The string is loaded with mime type `text/html` at ReportWebViewActivity.kt:88 into a WebView with JavaScript enabled.

`offlineIntent` has no caller in the tree, but `renderOffline` is also the default branch of `onCreate` — reached whenever EXTRA_URL is absent (ReportWebViewActivity.kt:59-68) — so the sink is not gated on that factory.

scope.established_by: Compared the two interpolations in the same template literal; one is encoded and one is not, then read what base URL the result is loaded under.

findings.title: /v1/manifest ingests into any tenant named in the request body, discarding the authenticated principal
findings.class: CWE-863 incorrect authorization / cross-tenant write (LLM01:2025, API1:2023)
findings.evidence: app.py:198 calls `await _require_principal(request)` and discards the result — the return value is not bound to a name. app.py:200 then passes the raw body straight to `ingest.consume_manifest(body.get('entries', []))`, with no jsonschema validation (contrast `/v1/documents`, which validates DOCUMENT_SCHEMA at app.py:179). ingest.py:96-103 reads the tenant from the entry itself: `_persist_chunks(entry['tenant_id'], ...)`. The sibling endpoint binds it correctly, `tenant_id=principal.tenant_id` at app.py:185. Any key that authenticates reaches this, including the public playground key at settings.py:47, whose principal is built at app.py:56-57.
findings.impact: Any caller holding any valid key — including the sandbox key printed in the public documentation — writes arbitrary chunks into any other tenant's `tenant-docs` collection. Those chunks are retrieved for that tenant's users and rendered into the model's system message by prompt.py:38, so this is a cross-tenant indirect prompt-injection channel against an agent that holds `http_get`. The attacker supplies the instructions and the victim's tenant supplies the data and the egress.
findings.recommendation: Bind the ingest to the caller: keep the principal and pass `principal.tenant_id`, ignoring any tenant field in the entry. Validate the manifest body against a schema like the document endpoint does, and if the shared-drive connector legitimately writes for many tenants, give it a distinct principal type authorised for that and check it explicitly.

triage.reason: No later layer re-checks tenancy: `_persist_chunks` (ingest.py:52-78) inserts exactly what it is given, and the only collection check, `_assert_collection`, is not called on this path at all.
`entry['tenant_id']` comes from the request body parsed at app.py:199.
The tenant is the boundary the whole service is organised around — retriever.py:56 forces it into every query — so a second principal plainly exists.
The route is registered on the shipped RouteTableDef and served by `build_app` (app.py:262-265).

scope.established_by: Compared the two ingestion routes: one binds tenant from the principal and validates a schema, the other discards the principal and validates nothing.

findings.title: Manifest ingestion defaults every chunk ACL to the wildcard that grants all principals
findings.class: CWE-276 incorrect default permissions
findings.evidence: ingest.py:100 supplies `entry.get('acl', ['*'])` when the entry omits an ACL. retriever.py:31-34 short-circuits on that value: `if '*' in chunk_acl: return True`, before the group intersection is considered. The HTTP document endpoint takes the opposite default, `[principal.tenant_id]` at app.py:189, and its schema forbids a wildcard entirely — DOCUMENT_SCHEMA constrains ACL items to `^[a-z0-9_-]{2,40}$` (app.py:41), which `*` does not match. The manifest path applies no schema at all.
findings.impact: Any manifest entry that omits an ACL becomes readable by every principal that can search the collection, bypassing the group model. Combined with the unbound tenant on the same endpoint, an attacker's injected chunks are not merely present in the victim tenant's corpus, they are guaranteed to be retrievable by every user in it.
findings.recommendation: Make the default deny — an absent ACL should raise, or fall back to the narrowest group, never to `*`. Apply the same schema to manifest entries that the document endpoint applies, so the wildcard is unrepresentable on both paths rather than only one.

triage.reason: `_acl_allows` is the only ACL control and the wildcard is its first branch (retriever.py:32); the SQL at retriever.py:59 does not filter on acl at all.
Tenancy still narrows the row, but within the tenant the wildcard removes the group narrowing entirely — and the companion finding removes the tenant narrowing too.
The docstring at ingest.py:92-93 asserts the connector supplies the ACL, which is precisely why the fallback is never exercised in testing and is unbounded when it is.

scope.established_by: Compared the ACL default on both ingestion paths and traced the wildcard value to the branch that honours it.

findings.title: The idempotency replay cache is not scoped to a tenant, so one tenant is served another's cached answer
findings.class: CWE-524 cross-tenant information exposure through caching (API1:2023)
findings.evidence: limits.py:37 builds the slot as `f'replay:{idempotency_key}'` with no principal component — contrast the rate-limit bucket in the same file's caller, which is namespaced by tenant at app.py:144 (`f'query:{principal.tenant_id}'`). app.py:153-157 consults the cache before producing an answer and returns the stored payload directly, and app.py:168 stores it. The payload built at app.py:110-114 contains the generated answer, the citations (source URLs and collection names, prompt.py:48-52) and the originating `tenant_id`.
findings.impact: A caller who presents an `Idempotency-Key` that another tenant used receives that tenant's answer, its source URLs and its tenant identifier, without any retrieval running and therefore without any of the tenancy enforcement at retriever.py:56 applying. Keys are client-chosen strings, so collisions are both guessable and forgeable.
findings.recommendation: Include the principal in the slot — tenant and subject — and additionally verify that a recalled payload's `tenant_id` matches the caller before returning it, so a key collision cannot cross a boundary even if the namespacing is later changed.

triage.reason: Nothing narrows the key: `replay_slot` takes only the client-supplied string (limits.py:35) and both call sites (app.py:155, app.py:168) pass it alone.
The cached return at app.py:157 happens before `answer()` is called, so retriever.py's tenant predicate is never reached on a hit.
The cached value is an answer synthesised from that tenant's private documents, together with the source URLs it cited.

scope.established_by: Compared the two key constructions in the request path; the rate-limit bucket carries the tenant and the replay slot does not.

findings.title: Caller-supplied conversation history is inserted into the model messages with an unvalidated role
findings.class: CWE-20 improper input validation / direct prompt injection (LLM01:2025)
findings.evidence: QUERY_SCHEMA constrains `history` to an array of at most 20 items (app.py:27) and specifies nothing about the items themselves — no `items` keyword, so any element shape validates. app.py:164 forwards `body.get('history')` and prompt.py:41-42 appends each turn verbatim: `{'role': turn['role'], 'content': turn['content']}`. A caller therefore submits `{'role': 'system', 'content': '...'}` and has it placed after the real system message at prompt.py:38 and before the user question at prompt.py:44.
findings.impact: Any client injects additional system-role instructions into the answering turn, overriding the citation and refusal rules in SYSTEM_INSTRUCTIONS and directing the tool loop — including `http_get`, which reaches any URL. The schema's presence is what makes this invisible: `history` looks validated, and only the array itself is.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the items in the schema: `items` with `role` restricted to an enum of `user` and `assistant`, `content` a bounded string, and `additionalProperties` false. Do not let a client supply a system-role message at all.

triage.reason: The narrowing that exists — `maxItems: 20` at app.py:27 — bounds the count and not the content; no condition anywhere restricts the role field.
The value arrives in the request body at app.py:147 and reaches prompt.py:42 unmodified.
The sink is the messages array passed to `client.chat.completions.create` at app.py:102-106, where role semantics are honoured by the model.

scope.established_by: Read the schema keyword by keyword against the fields the handler forwards, then followed `history` to the message assembly.

findings.title: Retrieved document text is concatenated into the system message with no separation between instructions and data
findings.class: CWE-77 / indirect prompt injection (LLM01:2025)
findings.impact: Text inside a retrieved document is read by the model with the same authority as the operator's own system instructions. Because the system prompt at prompt.py:15-18 explicitly directs the model to call `http_get` on links the context points at, an injected chunk that says so causes the service to fetch an attacker URL and, by embedding retrieved content in the query string, to exfiltrate it.
findings.recommendation: Move retrieved context out of the system role into a separate user- or tool-role message, wrap each chunk in an explicit delimiter, and state in the system instructions that context blocks are data and their contents are never instructions. Remove the standing direction to follow links.

triage.reason: No output or input filter exists anywhere in the service: there is no moderation call, no injection classifier, and `dispatch` (tools.py:97-109) executes whatever tool the model names.
`hit.text` is the stored chunk, written through `/v1/documents` (app.py:183) or `/v1/manifest` (app.py:200); both are caller-supplied.
The sink is the system role of the completion request (app.py:104), which is the highest-authority position in the message list.

scope.established_by: AI-01 lethal-trifecta check run first: private tenant data via retriever.search, untrusted content via ingested chunks, external communication via http_get — all three present in one agent, and this is the leg that joins the first two.

findings.title: The http_get tool fetches any URL the model names, with no scheme, host or address restriction
findings.class: CWE-918 server-side request forgery (LLM06:2025, A10:2021)
findings.evidence: tools.py:20-26 takes `url` and performs `session.get(url)` with no validation: no scheme allowlist, no host allowlist, no resolution of the target address, no rejection of private or link-local ranges, and no redirect cap. The `principal` argument is accepted and never used, so the fetch is not scoped to the caller in any way. The tool is registered and offered to the model at tools.py:68-76 and tools.py:92, and the system prompt instructs the model to use it on links the context points at (prompt.py:16-17). `dispatch` (tools.py:109) calls it with whatever arguments the model produced.
findings.impact: Two effects on one primitive. Outbound: retrieved content is exfiltrated by asking the model to fetch an attacker URL with the data in the query string, and only 4000 characters of the response return to the model while the whole request reaches the attacker. Inbound: the service reaches anything its network position can — cloud instance metadata, the internal model gateway at settings.py:27, the warehouse and the settlement services — and returns up to 4000 characters of the response into the conversation.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the tool to an allowlist of hosts derived from the `source_url` values of the chunks actually retrieved for this turn, resolve the host and reject private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses before connecting, disable redirects, and cap the response size. If arbitrary fetching is genuinely required, move it to an isolated egress proxy with its own allowlist.

triage.reason: No egress control is declared anywhere in the component: `aiohttp.ClientSession` is constructed at tools.py:23 with only a timeout, and no proxy setting or network policy accompanies the service.
The URL is produced by the model from context an attacker can write (ingest.py:73) and passed through `json.loads` at tools.py:104 into the call at tools.py:109.
Fetching linked documents is intended, but nothing bounds which host may be reached, which is what FP-05 requires.

scope.established_by: AI-01: this is the external-communication leg of the trifecta. Enumerated every outbound call in the component — one — and every guard on it — none.

findings.title: The session JWT signing key falls back to a literal committed in source when the environment variable is unset
findings.class: CWE-798 hardcoded credential / fail-open default secret
findings.evidence: config.ts:23 falls back to a readable English literal committed in the repository (redacted here). The same value is bound at module load on both sides of the trust boundary: session.ts:9 encodes it and session.ts:55 signs with it, while auth.ts:20 encodes it and auth.ts:26 verifies with it. The fallback is silent — nothing in src/ validates the value and nothing branches on the environment except the proxy-identity flag.
findings.impact: If the variable is absent from the runtime environment, the API signs and verifies its own session tokens with a key that is public in the source tree. Anyone holding the repository mints a token with arbitrary organisation, role and crew claims and it verifies. The service boots and serves normally, so there is no operational signal that it happened.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback and fail closed at boot: read the variable with no default and throw if it is missing or shorter than 32 bytes, before the pool or the router are constructed. Treat the committed literal as burned and rotate it.

triage.reason: Not a placeholder in the FP-02 sense: a template marker breaks loudly, while this literal is consumed as a working key and produces valid tokens. The file is application configuration, not an example template.
config.ts is compiled by the build script and executed by the start script; the fallback is evaluated at runtime in every environment.
The verifier uses the same key object; there is no key id, no issuer allowlist against an external key set and no server-side session record.

The comment at config.ts:3-5 asserts the deployed stacks override these through the task environment, but that is prose rather than an exported artifact, and the infrastructure in this tree does not corroborate it — pulumi-platform creates no task definition or container environment at all. FP-08 requires the artifact, so this stays UNKNOWN and caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Symbol census across the component returned exactly three sites; both consumers capture the value once at module scope, so every mint and verify in the process uses it.

findings.title: Legacy /files mount serves attachments with no authentication and no tenancy check
findings.class: CWE-306 missing authentication / CWE-639 IDOR (A01:2021)
findings.evidence: index.ts:28 protects the versioned tree with `app.use('/api/v1/*', requireAuth)`. The legacy mount at index.ts:35 uses `attachActor` instead, which auth.ts:74-78 defines as: resolve the actor if a bearer is present, then `await next()` unconditionally. index.ts:36 then mounts the same attachments router at `/files`. Inside it, attachments.ts:80 and attachments.ts:97 both gate on `if (actor && actor.orgId !== row.orgId)` — with no token the actor is undefined, the condition short-circuits to false, and no 403 is raised. `GET /files/<id>` returns metadata and `GET /files/<id>/raw` streams the bytes, for any attachment id in any organisation, with no credential.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated read of every stored attachment across every tenant — customer site photos, signature captures and any document a technician uploaded — by iterating attachment ids.
findings.recommendation: Mount the legacy prefix behind `requireAuth` like the versioned tree, and invert the two conditionals to fail closed: `if (!actor || actor.orgId !== row.orgId) return 403`. If unauthenticated pre-signed links are genuinely required, verify a signature on the link rather than allowing an absent actor to skip the check.

triage.reason: No other layer authenticates this path: index.ts:35 is the only middleware on the `/files` prefix and it is the soft variant; the per-row check at attachments.ts:80/97 is the control being skipped.
The mount is unconditional at index.ts:35-36 with `config.legacyFilesMount` defaulting to '/files' (config.ts:32); no environment flag removes it.
The boundary is the organisation: rows carry `org_id` and the versioned path enforces it, so a second principal plainly exists.
Nothing narrows the mount; `app.route(config.legacyFilesMount, attachments)` exposes the whole router including the raw-bytes route.

scope.established_by: Compared the middleware attached to each mount in index.ts, then read every authorization conditional in the attachments router.

findings.title: The brute-force limiter guards /session/login while /session/token performs the same credential check unlimited
findings.class: CWE-307 improper restriction of authentication attempts (A07:2021)
findings.evidence: index.ts:24 applies `loginLimiter` to exactly one path: `/api/v1/session/login`. session.ts:84-96 exposes `POST /token` which, for `grantType: 'password'`, calls the identical `findPrincipal` + `passwordMatches` pair (session.ts:91-92) that `/login` calls at session.ts:66-67, and returns a usable token at session.ts:95. No limiter is mounted on it. `POST /recover` (session.ts:111) is likewise unlimited. The limiter itself is the only such control in the tree: `rateLimit` has one other export and no other call site.
findings.impact: The rate limit that exists to stop password guessing is bypassed by sending the guess to a sibling endpoint on the same router. Credential stuffing against the whole principal table proceeds at request speed, and the unlimited /recover endpoint additionally allows account enumeration by timing and unbounded recovery-mail generation.
findings.recommendation: Apply the limiter to the router rather than to one path — `app.use('/api/v1/session/*', loginLimiter)` — and add a per-account failure counter with lockout, since an IP-keyed window does not stop a distributed attempt.

triage.reason: No account lockout or secondary throttle exists: `principals` is read at session.ts:31-35 with no failure counter, and the only limiter is the one mounted at index.ts:24.
This is the inverse of a narrowing: the guard's scope is narrower than the surface it must cover, and the uncovered sibling is registered on the same router at index.ts:25.
session.ts:84 is a shipped route on the public session router mounted at index.ts:25.

scope.established_by: Listed every route on the session router and joined it against every middleware mount in index.ts; one of three credential-touching routes is covered.

findings.title: The dispatch-board cache key omits the crew dimension, so a tech is served another crew's rows
findings.class: CWE-524 information exposure through caching (A01:2021)
findings.evidence: cache.ts:11 builds the key from organisation, status and page only. The query the key caches is not a function of those three: workorders.ts:60 computes `visibleCrewFilter(actor)`, which policy.ts:47-50 returns as the actor's crew list for a `tech` and null for everyone else, and workorders.ts:67-70 appends `and crew_id = any(...)` when it is non-null. So two callers with different crew scopes share one cache slot. A manager or dispatcher requesting the board first stores the unfiltered organisation-wide result at workorders.ts:76; a tech requesting the same status and page then hits at workorders.ts:54-58 and receives rows for crews outside their filter, with the response marked `x-cache: hit`.
findings.impact: Cross-crew disclosure of work-order records — including the free-text notes field, which policy.ts:53-55 documents as routinely containing pasted customer correspondence — to technicians the crew filter exists to exclude. It is racy rather than deterministic, which makes it likely to be dismissed as a display glitch.
findings.recommendation: Include the authorization scope in the key: append a stable digest of the crew filter (or the role plus sorted crew ids) in `listKey`, so a differently scoped caller cannot collide. Caching an authorization-dependent response under a key that omits the authorization input is the defect class, not this instance.

triage.reason: Nothing narrows the slot: `listKey` takes three arguments (cache.ts:11) and the only call site (workorders.ts:53) passes org, status and page, none of which encodes the crew filter.
The cache read at workorders.ts:54-58 returns before the SQL is built, so the crew predicate at workorders.ts:67-70 is not reached on a hit.
The cached payload is the full work-order rows selected at workorders.ts:62-63, including `notes` and `assignedTo`.

scope.established_by: Compared the inputs to the cache key against the inputs to the SQL predicate for the same response; the predicate depends on actor role and crews, the key does not.

findings.title: Identity is taken from client-settable x-fieldops-* headers whenever NODE_ENV is production
findings.class: CWE-290 authentication bypass by spoofing (A07:2021)
findings.evidence: config.ts:28 sets `trustProxyIdentity` true exactly when NODE_ENV === 'production'. auth.ts:59-61 then falls back to `fromProxyHeaders` when no valid bearer is present, and auth.ts:46-52 builds the actor from `x-fieldops-actor`, `x-fieldops-org`, `x-fieldops-role` and `x-fieldops-crews` read straight off the request. Nothing strips a client-supplied copy: the load balancer that is supposed to set them is declared in this same tree at pulumi-platform/edge.ts:35 with `dropInvalidHeaderFields: false`, and its comment at edge.ts:32-34 states the listener passes request headers through untouched. No mutual-TLS trust store is configured anywhere in pulumi-platform.
findings.impact: In production, any client that can reach the load balancer authenticates as any user in any organisation by setting three headers, and `x-fieldops-role: admin` grants the admin role that policy.ts:37 short-circuits every site check for. This is a complete authentication and authorization bypass requiring no credential.
findings.recommendation: Terminate client certificates properly and derive the principal from the verified certificate, or drop the header path entirely. Whatever remains must be preceded by a hop that unconditionally strips inbound `x-fieldops-*` headers so only the trusted terminator can set them.

triage.reason: The ALB configuration is in this tree and does the opposite of compensating: pulumi-platform/edge.ts:35 disables `dropInvalidHeaderFields` and no WAF rule in edge.ts:159-189 inspects these headers.
The values are request headers read at auth.ts:46-52 on a listener open to 0.0.0.0/0 per pulumi-platform/network.ts:76.
Unusually this can be answered from the tree rather than left UNKNOWN: the proxy in question is defined in pulumi-platform/edge.ts and its header handling is declared there.

scope.established_by: Traced `trustProxyIdentity` from its definition to its single reader, then joined the header names to the ALB declaration in the sibling infrastructure component.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldops-api/src/config.ts:28 — the fallback is active only when NODE_ENV is exactly 'production', which is the deployed configuration.

findings.title: The refresh-token grant does not exclude disabled principals, so deprovisioning does not take effect
findings.class: CWE-613 insufficient session expiration (A07:2021)
findings.evidence: `findPrincipal`, used by both password paths, filters on `disabled_at is null` (session.ts:33). The refresh branch does not use it: session.ts:98-104 issues its own query joining `refresh_tokens` to `principals` with the predicates `r.token = $1 and r.expires_at > now()` and no `disabled_at` condition. session.ts:107 then mints a fresh 900-second token from that row.
findings.impact: Disabling an account stops password sign-in but not the refresh grant. A terminated employee, or an attacker holding a stolen refresh token, keeps minting valid session tokens for as long as the refresh row lives, and each new token carries the org, role and crew claims from the principals row. Account revocation, the control an incident response depends on, silently does not work.
findings.recommendation: Add `and p.disabled_at is null` to the join at session.ts:102, and delete the principal's refresh rows when the account is disabled so revocation is immediate rather than dependent on the next mint.

triage.reason: No later check re-tests the account state: session.ts:105-107 goes straight from the row to `mintToken`, and `requireAuth` (auth.ts:57-67) validates only the token signature, never the principal record.
The query's two predicates narrow by token value and expiry only; neither is the account-state condition present on the sibling path at session.ts:33.
The refresh branch is the default arm of a shipped route (session.ts:84) reached whenever grantType is 'refresh'.

scope.established_by: Diffed the two principal-lookup queries in the file; the shared helper carries the account-state filter and the inline refresh query does not.

findings.title: Arbitrary JavaScript execution through the work-order print template query parameter
findings.class: CWE-94 code injection (A03:2021)
findings.evidence: workorders.ts:185 reads `const template = c.req.query('template') ?? DEFAULT_SHEET` directly off the raw query string, then workorders.ts:186 compiles it: `new Function('wo', 'return `'+template+'`;')` and calls it at line 191. A template literal evaluates `${...}`, so `?template=${process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')}` runs arbitrary code in the API process. The zod schema at workorders.ts:164-168 is `.strict()` but governs only `c.req.valid('query')`; the raw `c.req.query('template')` read never passes through it.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller, including the lowest-privileged `tech`, reaches remote code execution in the API container. That container's task role is the settlement-worker role in the shared account, which pulumi-platform/iam.ts:46 grants Action:'*' on Resource:'*'.
findings.recommendation: Delete the runtime template compilation. If per-org sheet layouts are required, select a named layout from a server-side allowlist keyed by org, and render with a logic-less templating engine that interpolates values rather than evaluating expressions.

triage.reason: The value is read from the request query string at workorders.ts:185; no allowlist or constant constrains it.
The sink is `new Function` (workorders.ts:186), which compiles and executes; it is not a parser or a text sink.
The route is registered on the shipped router mounted at index.ts:29 and built by `npm run build` (package.json:9).
printQuery `.strict()` at workorders.ts:168 narrows only the validated object; the sink reads the unvalidated raw query, so the narrowing never applies to it.

scope.established_by: Traced `template` from the raw query read to the `new Function` construction and its invocation inside the HTML assembly.

findings.title: PATCH on a work order omits the site-clearance and crew checks that POST enforces
findings.class: CWE-863 incorrect authorization (A01:2021, API5:2023)
findings.evidence: The create handler runs two gates: `sameOrgSite` at workorders.ts:89 and `canWriteSite` at workorders.ts:92. The update handler checks only that the row is in the caller's org (workorders.ts:123) and, if and only if a new siteId is supplied, `sameOrgSite` at workorders.ts:133. `canWriteSite` is never called on the update path — grep across src/ returns exactly two occurrences, the import at workorders.ts:7 and the call at workorders.ts:92. There is also no crew narrowing: `visibleCrewFilter` (workorders.ts:60) restricts what a `tech` can list, but PATCH addresses a row by id with no equivalent, so a tech can modify work orders belonging to crews they cannot see.
findings.impact: Any authenticated member of an organisation can rewrite any work order in it — title, notes, assigned crew and status — regardless of role, crew membership or site clearance. A `tech` whose `canWriteSite` would return false (policy.ts:39 returns false for every role that is not admin, manager or dispatcher) is nevertheless free to reassign and close work across the whole organisation.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same pair of gates on the update path, and add the crew predicate to the row lookup at workorders.ts:117 so a tech can only address rows `visibleCrewFilter` would have returned. Better, route both handlers through one authorization function so a new writer cannot be added without it.

triage.reason: No middleware supplies the missing check: index.ts:28 attaches only `requireAuth`, and `requireRole` (auth.ts:81) has no call site anywhere in src/.
The org check at workorders.ts:123 narrows to the tenant but not to the crew or the cleared site, which are the two dimensions POST additionally enforces.
The second principal is another crew inside the same organisation, a boundary the list handler enforces at workorders.ts:60-70 and the update handler does not.

scope.established_by: Grouped the two writers of the work_orders entity and diffed their guard sequences line by line; the create path runs two checks, the update path one conditional check.

Every other value in the same HTML document is escaped — `escapeHtml(wo.id)` at workorders.ts:189, `wo.title` at :192, `wo.siteId` at :194, `wo.status` at :195 — while workorders.ts:197 emits `

` raw. The only sanitiser on the write path is `scrubNotes` (policy.ts:57-63), a three-pattern blacklist: it removes `` pairs, iframe tags and the literal `javascript:`. It does not touch event-handler attributes, so `` and `

findings.title: The analytics read replica is publicly addressed in public subnets with 5432 open to the internet

location.symbol: analytics replica and its ingress rule

findings.class: CWE-1327 binding to an unrestricted address
findings.evidence: data.ts:54-57 builds the replica subnet group from the public subnets, which set public IP on launch at network.ts:51 and route to the internet gateway at network.ts:30-33. data.ts:64 sets the instance publicly accessible. data.ts:71-78 adds a security group ingress rule on the shared database group with the whole internet as the source on the database port.
findings.impact: A full replica of the transactional database answers on its port from any address on the internet, with only the master credential in the way. The same rule widens the group shared with the primary, so a later move of the primary into a public subnet needs no further change.
findings.recommendation: Make the replica private and non-public, and replace the open rule with a dedicated group accepting the port only from a managed prefix list or a private endpoint — and keep it off the group the primary uses.

triage.reason: No network ACL, managed firewall or other layer is declared anywhere in the ten files.
The procedure's exculpation covers a public load balancer on web ports; this is a database port. The stated reason — an unreliable vendor egress list — explains the choice but bounds nothing.
The rule carries no narrowing: no source group, no prefix list, no condition. Its description names two consumers but constrains neither.

scope.established_by: Followed the public subnet ids from the network module into the replica declaration, then joined the replica's security group to the ingress rule's group id.

findings.title: The /internal/* listener rule forwards to the console target group without the OIDC authentication its sibling applies
findings.class: CWE-306 missing authentication for critical function
findings.evidence: edge.ts:102-122 routes the console prefix through an authenticate-oidc action at edge.ts:108 before forwarding. edge.ts:127-132 routes a second prefix to the same target group at edge.ts:131 with a single forward action and no authenticate action. The comment at edge.ts:100-101 states the console container has no login of its own. The ALB web ACL carries exactly one rule, matching a different prefix at edge.ts:169.
findings.impact: Any host on the internet — the ALB security group admits 0.0.0.0/0 on 443 per network.ts:76 — reaches the dispatch console backend by using the unauthenticated prefix instead of the authenticated one, against a container stated to have no authentication of its own.
findings.recommendation: Attach the same authenticate-oidc action to the rule with unauthenticated requests denied, or remove the rule and give the monitoring integration a separate target group with its own credential check.

triage.reason: No unskippable layer authenticates it: the ALB web ACL holds one rule whose match string is a different prefix, and the CloudFront ACL that does block this prefix is scoped to CloudFront and bound to the reports distribution, not to the ALB.
No condition narrows the rule: edge.ts:130 matches the whole prefix with no source, header or IP-set condition, unlike the sibling rule that is narrowed at edge.ts:159-189.
The comment names the intent but nothing bounds who may use the prefix; the listener is reachable from the whole internet.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all four listener rules on the HTTPS listener and compared their action lists and target groups.

findings.title: The load balancer passes client-settable identity headers straight to the target group
findings.class: CWE-290 authentication bypass by spoofing
findings.evidence: edge.ts:32-34 records that the dispatcher fleet's client-certificate identity reaches the application as a set of custom headers, so the listener passes request headers through untouched, and edge.ts:35 disables the invalid-header drop. The listener is reachable from the whole internet per network.ts:76, and no listener rule, WAF rule or function strips or overwrites those headers — the ALB web ACL carries one rule matching an unrelated prefix. No mutual-TLS trust store is configured anywhere in the program.
findings.impact: The application in this same tree trusts exactly these headers: fieldops-api/src/middleware/auth.ts:46-52 builds the actor from them whenever the environment is production. So any internet client sets three headers and authenticates as any user in any organisation, with the role of its choosing.
findings.recommendation: Terminate client certificates properly with a trust store so the identity is derived from a verified certificate, and add a rule that strips inbound copies of these headers so only the trusted terminator can set them. Enable the invalid-header drop as a secondary step.

triage.reason: The consuming application does not re-validate: the sibling component's middleware accepts the headers as an identity source with no signature or secondary check.
The header value is fully attacker-controlled: it arrives on a request to a listener open to the internet and no declared component rewrites it.
No route-level narrowing exists; the pass-through is set on the load balancer itself and therefore applies to every listener rule.

scope.established_by: The setting is on the load balancer resource, so it applies to every rule on both listeners; the consuming code was located in the sibling API component.

findings.title: Fallback policy grants Action '*' on Resource '*' to the settlement-worker task role
findings.class: CWE-732 incorrect permission assignment / IAM least privilege
findings.evidence: iam.ts:50-55 lists four services; the policy record at iam.ts:15-42 defines only three keys. iam.ts:80 resolves the missing one to the bootstrap statement at iam.ts:46, an Allow of every action on every resource, which iam.ts:82-85 attaches as an inline role policy. The role at iam.ts:66-78 declares no permissions boundary.
findings.impact: The settlement worker runs with administrator-equivalent rights in the account: it can read every bucket including the reports and export buckets, read every secret, create IAM principals and disable logging. Compromise of one container is compromise of the whole shared footprint in both environments.
findings.recommendation: Delete the bootstrap fallback and make the lookup fail closed, throwing on an unmapped service, then add an explicit least-privilege entry for the missing one. Attach a permissions boundary to every role created in the loop.

triage.reason: No compensating layer is declared in the ten files: no permissions boundary on the role, no service control policy, and no resource-account or principal-tag condition in the statement.
Nothing bounds it: the comment at iam.ts:44 calls it temporary, but iam.ts:54 keeps the service on that path in both stacks and neither stack file gates it.
There is no narrowing condition; iam.ts:46 carries no Condition key at all.

scope.established_by: Cross-referenced the services array key by key against the policy record keys; exactly one is absent, and index.ts:43 calls the factory for every stack.

findings.title: The staging exports bucket is world-readable while production export objects are replicated into it
findings.class: CWE-668 exposure of resource to wrong sphere
findings.evidence: Pulumi.staging.yaml:9 enables the public-exports flag, so storage.ts:44-47 evaluates all four block flags to false and storage.ts:50-68 attaches a bucket policy granting anonymous object reads on every key. Pulumi.staging.yaml:12 additionally enables replication, so storage.ts:70-89 accepts inbound replication from the production account role into that same bucket. The bucket is tagged as holding work-order and billing exports at storage.ts:29.
findings.impact: Production work-order and billing export objects land in a bucket whose public access block is fully disabled and whose policy grants anonymous reads on every key. Anyone who learns or guesses the bucket name reads production customer and billing data without credentials, and the name derives predictably from the tenant slug and environment.
findings.recommendation: Never derive a public access block from a feature flag — keep all four flags hard-coded true and serve sample exports through a presigned URL or the distribution. If public sample data is required, use a separate bucket that replication never targets, and make the two flags mutually exclusive.

triage.reason: The only declared access control for this bucket is the public access block, and the stack config is what turns it off; no account or organisation control is declared in the ten files.
Public read is intended but not bounded: the replication flag writes production export objects into it.
The tag at storage.ts:29 identifies the contents as work-order and billing exports, and the replication comment states they are the same objects partners work against in production.

Even if the replication policy wins the write race with the public policy, storage.ts:44-47 still leaves all four block flags false, so a public ACL or a reapplied policy makes the bucket public with no further change.

scope.established_by: Read both stack config files key by key and traced the two flags through index.ts into the storage module.
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 sets both flags false, so the exposure is the staging stack holding replicated production objects.

findings.title: The HMAC covers the message body but not the type field that selects the handler
findings.class: CWE-345 / CWE-347 improper verification of cryptographic signature
findings.evidence: consumer.py:61 builds the entry as type, body and sig, where `sig = _signature(body)` — the routing field is outside the signed material. consumer.py:69-72 verifies only `body`, then consumer.py:75 sets `msg['type']` from the unsigned field and consumer.py:89 dispatches on it. Anyone able to append to the stream can re-post an observed (body, sig) pair under `type="payout.reissue"` and the signature still verifies. retry.py:26 repeats the pattern. The signed body carries no nonce or timestamp (consumer.py:60), so an old capture stays valid indefinitely.
findings.impact: A captured, validly signed payout is re-routed to a handler with different authorization and idempotency semantics — reaching `handle_payout_reissue`, which has no scope check and no idempotency lookup, for unlimited repeat settlement of a message legitimately signed once.
findings.recommendation: Sign the whole entry, or move `type` inside the signed body and ignore the field on the entry. Add a nonce or issued-at timestamp to the signed body and reject stale or repeated ones.

triage.reason: The HMAC at consumer.py:70 is the only integrity control on the entry and its input is `body` alone; nothing else reads `type` before dispatch at consumer.py:89.
`type` is read from the stream entry at consumer.py:75 and retry.py:26, not from a constant.
Producer signing establishes the stream writer as a separate principal.

scope.established_by: Traced the arguments of `_signature` against the fields dict built at consumer.py:61 and the dispatch key at consumer.py:89.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires the ability to append to the settlement stream; a deployment ACL was not in scope.

findings.title: The consume path never validates against PayoutRequest, so amount bounds and destination checks apply only to the publisher
findings.class: CWE-20 improper input validation / CWE-841 improper enforcement of behavioral workflow
findings.evidence: consumer.py:74 does `msg = json.loads(body)` and returns a bare dict; `PayoutRequest` appears in consumer.py only in the import and the two publish-side signatures (lines 44, 54), never applied to a consumed message. So `Field(gt=0, le=MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS)` at schemas.py:27 governs nothing on this path. Handlers take the value raw at handlers.py:44, 94 and 117, and `LedgerEntry.amount_cents` (schemas.py:41) declares no bound. A `payout.cancel` message posts a positive amount to the message's own destination account, and `post_entry` (ledger.py:65) can refuse a movement that would make a balance negative but cannot refuse a credit. `_destination_is_registered` (consumer.py:44-51) is called only from `publish_payout`.
findings.impact: An arbitrary credit of any size to any syntactically valid account, reachable by a single actor holding the ordinary payouts:write scope. The declared ceiling and the positive-amount rule are enforced on the wrong side of the trust boundary.
findings.recommendation: Validate in `decode` with `PayoutRequest.model_validate(json.loads(body))` and pass the model, not a dict, to the handlers. Put the same bound on `LedgerEntry.amount_cents` and re-run `_destination_is_registered` on the consume side.

triage.reason: The only bound is on the publisher's model; the dead-letter replay path and any direct stream writer both reach handlers.py:44 without it.
`amount_cents` and `destination_account` come from the stream body parsed at consumer.py:74.
`LedgerEntry` narrows tenant, account, currency and reference by pattern but declares `amount_cents` as a bare int, so the narrowing does not reach the value at issue.

scope.established_by: Traced `json.loads` forward to every `int(msg[...])` site and counted PayoutRequest references, all publish-side.
scope.narrowed_by: The amount must pass `int()`; a non-numeric value raises and lands in the dead-letter queue, which is itself the first finding's path.

findings.title: handle_payout_reissue moves money with no scope check and no idempotency lookup while its three siblings have both
findings.class: CWE-862 / CWE-863 missing and incorrect authorization
findings.evidence: `handle_payout` (handlers.py:78), `handle_payout_cancel` (:92) and `handle_refund` (:115) each open with `_require_scope`. `handle_payout_reissue` (handlers.py:107-111) opens with neither: handlers.py:109 calls the same `_apply_payout` that `handle_payout` reaches at :86, and handlers.py:110 calls `idempotency.remember` without the `idempotency.lookup` that guards `handle_payout` at :81-84. Dispatch is a plain dict of functions (consumer.py:26-31) called at consumer.py:95 — no decorator, base class or middleware wraps it.
findings.impact: Any message routed as `payout.reissue` settles a payout regardless of the actor's scopes, and settles it again on every redelivery because the replay guard is written but never read.
findings.recommendation: Add `_require_scope(msg, "payouts:write")` as the first statement and the same lookup-and-return-cached prologue `handle_payout` uses. Better, make the guarded prologue a decorator applied at the handler table so a new handler cannot be registered without one.

triage.reason: consumer.py:95 calls the handler directly out of the dict at consumer.py:26-31; nothing wraps it.
No external control was claimed for this path.
The effect is identical, not merely similar: handlers.py:109 and :86 call the same function with the same message.

scope.established_by: Listed every use of `_require_scope` (one definition, three calls) against the four handlers registered at consumer.py:26-31.

findings.title: Replay protection is check-then-act, records the receipt after the money has moved, and the atomic primitive is never called
findings.class: CWE-367 time-of-check to time-of-use / CWE-362 race condition
findings.evidence: Three replay windows on one key. Race: handlers.py:81 reads the slot and handlers.py:87 writes it with the ledger movements in between at :86, so two workers picking up the same key both see None and both settle. `idempotency.claim` (idempotency.py:42-44) is the atomic SET NX that would close this and has zero callers; it would not work if wired, because it stores an empty object which `lookup` turns into an empty dict and handlers.py:82 tests with a truthiness check. Ordering: money is posted at handlers.py:46-63 before `remember` at :87, so a failure in between leaves the movement applied with no receipt and the entry then dead-letters for replay. Atomicity: `post_entry` writes Redis (ledger.py:71) and Postgres (ledger.py:78) separately and `_apply_payout` posts two legs with no transaction. `handle_payout_cancel` and `handle_refund` never consult idempotency at all. consumer.py:81 creates the group at id 0, so a recreated group redelivers the entire stream.
findings.impact: Double settlement of the same payout by several distinct routes, and half-applied double-entry movements that leave the ledger and the journal disagreeing.
findings.recommendation: Claim the slot atomically before any movement and convert it to the receipt only after both legs commit, releasing on failure. Test the cached value with an identity check rather than truthiness. Post both legs in one transaction with a unique constraint on `reference`, and create the group at the stream tail.

triage.reason: A unique constraint on the journal's reference column would make the second write fail, but no migration or DDL beyond ledger.py:19-24 is in scope and that block declares no constraint. This caps the finding at probable.
`handle_payout` is registered at consumer.py:27 and is the primary path.
`claim` and `release` are ordinary module functions with zero references outside their definitions, not framework hooks.

scope.established_by: Read the read-decide-write sequence at handlers.py:80-88 and counted callers of claim and release across the package.

findings.title: Reconciliation overwrites any account balance directly, bypassing the ledger gate, from a file nothing authenticates
findings.class: CWE-862 missing authorization / CWE-20 improper input validation
findings.evidence: ledger.py:3-4 documents `post_entry` as the single gate that refuses to leave an account negative. reconcile.py:56 does not use it: it sets the balance key outright. The values come from `csv.DictReader` at reconcile.py:44-47 with no validation — the tenant and account patterns at schemas.py:14-15 are never applied on this path, and the integer conversion accepts any magnitude and any sign. The journal row written beside it at reconcile.py:63 hardcodes the currency regardless of the account, and the loop at :69-73 has no transaction, so a malformed later row aborts the run with earlier balances already rewritten.
findings.impact: Whoever supplies the nightly statement file controls the authoritative balance of every account, with no ownership check, no signature on the file and no bound on the value — including setting a balance negative, which the ledger gate exists to prevent.
findings.recommendation: Reconciliation should post a delta through `post_entry` like every other movement, never set the key. Verify the statement file's origin before parsing, validate each row against the same models the message path uses, carry the row's real currency, and wrap the run in one transaction.

triage.reason: `post_entry` is the compensating control and reconcile.py:56 is written to go around it; no other layer reads balance keys before they are set.
Tenant, account and closing balance come from the CSV at reconcile.py:45-47, an external party's file per reconcile.py:1-5.
`reconcile.run` has no caller in scope and no console-script entry, so its trigger is outside what was given. This caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Grouped every writer of the balance entity by hand after the writer-parity tool returned no flags, since it groups by declared class or table and a Redis key is neither.

findings.title: Dead-letter replay applies payouts with neither signature verification nor authorization
findings.class: CWE-862 missing authorization / CWE-345 insufficient verification of data authenticity
