findings.evidence: An entry with a wrong or absent `sig` raises at consumer.py:69-72; consumer.py:114 catches every Exception, consumer.py:116 writes the entry verbatim to the dead-letter stream and consumer.py:117 acks it. The operator drain, shipped as the console script `settlement-retry` (pyproject.toml:16), rebuilds the message at retry.py:24-27 with `json.loads` and no HMAC — retry.py imports no `hmac` — and retry.py:43 calls the private `handlers._apply_payout(msg)` directly, skipping both `consumer.decode` and `_require_scope`. A Forbidden raised at handlers.py:31 takes the identical route.
findings.impact: Every control on the message path is bypassed by making a message fail once. Unsigned or unauthorized payout messages are quarantined rather than rejected, then applied in full by the drain job to any account and amount the message names.
findings.recommendation: Route the replay through the same funnel as live traffic: `consumer.decode(entry)` for signature verification, then `HANDLERS[msg['type']]` so scope checks and idempotency run. Never call `_apply_payout` from outside handlers.py, and reject entries that reached the dead-letter queue because of a signature or authorization failure rather than storing them for replay.

triage.reason: The only signature gate is consumer.py:69-72 inside `decode`; retry.py:43 does not call it and retry.py has no hmac import. The only scope gate is handlers.py:27-31, reached from the public handlers but not from `_apply_payout`.
pyproject.toml:16 ships this path as a console script; retry.py:64-72 is its main().
The HMAC at consumer.py:38-41 exists because stream writers are a second principal; settlement/__init__.py:4-5 names three distinct producers.
The replayed body is the untrusted stream entry stored at consumer.py:116.

scope.established_by: Symbol census: `decode` has three references, all in consumer.py; `_require_scope` has four in handlers.py and none in retry.py.

findings.title: Producer signature verification is switched off whenever the environment is staging, and staging reads the production stream
findings.class: CWE-345 / CWE-1188 insecure environment-dependent default
findings.evidence: settings.py:43 computes `verify_producer_signature = _env() != "staging"`; consumer.py:69 makes the whole HMAC check conditional on it. The comment immediately above, settings.py:32-33, states that staging reads the same stream, and the defaults confirm it: stream, group and dead-letter names are the same literals in every environment (settings.py:34-36), so a staging worker joins the production consumer group.
findings.impact: A worker for which any unsigned message is acceptable consumes production payout traffic. Unsigned messages are settled, and because the group name is shared the staging consumer also claims and acks production entries, which then never reach a production worker.
findings.recommendation: Verification is not an environment-dependent property. Keep it always on and give internal publishers a signing key of their own; if staging must be permissive, give it its own stream, group and dead-letter names so it cannot see production entries.

triage.reason: This is not a path production does not set — it is a deployed environment reading the production stream by design, per settings.py:32-33 and the shared defaults at :34-36.
Nothing else authenticates the producer; the HMAC at consumer.py:70 is the only such control.
Network segmentation between the staging worker and the production Redis would bound this, and no deployment artifact was in scope. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, which is why this ships as probable.

scope.established_by: Key-by-key enumeration of settings.py cross-referenced with the single reader of the flag.
scope.narrowed_by: Applies to processes started with the staging environment name; development and production get the check.

findings.title: The producer HMAC key defaults to an empty string and nothing fails closed
findings.class: CWE-347 / CWE-1188 / CWE-798 insecure default credential
findings.evidence: settings.py:38 defaults the secret to an empty string. Its only reader, consumer.py:40, builds an HMAC with an empty key when the variable is unset; consumer.py:69-72 then compares against a value any party can recompute from the body alone. There is no startup assertion, no length check and no refusal to run. The same key also authenticates the actor identity, since `_require_scope` (handlers.py:29) reads the actor from the signed body.
findings.impact: If the variable is missing in any environment, message authentication is decorative and every downstream control that trusts the body — actor identity, tenant, amount — trusts attacker input.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed at import: raise if the secret is empty or shorter than 32 bytes whenever verification is enabled. Remove the default entirely rather than defaulting to a value that silently disables the control.

triage.reason: No guard exists anywhere: the setting has exactly two occurrences in the tree, its declaration and its single reader.
The finding is the absence of a secret, not the exposure of one; no secret value is present in the repository.
A deployment that always injects the variable would bound this, and no deployment manifest exists anywhere under the target root. Absence of evidence is not HOLDS, so the finding ships as probable.

scope.established_by: Key-by-key enumeration of settings.py and a symbol census of its single reader.

findings.title: The partner export folder is the one folder with no row-security pre-hook, and the model has no tenant predicate
findings.class: CWE-1230 / cross-tenant exposure to a third party
findings.evidence: In dbt_project.yml the `staging` and `marts` folders each declare `+pre-hook: "{{ enable_row_security(this) }}"`; the `exports` folder declares only `+post-hook: "{{ apply_grants(this) }}"` and no pre-hook, so no `tenant_isolation` policy is ever created on the export relation. The model itself filters on one column only — `where p.partner_id = '{{ partner }}'` at partner_extract.sql:30 — while selecting `e.tenant_id` at :47, so rows for every tenant that transacts with that partner land in one table. The folder is then granted to `partner_readers` (dbt_project.yml exports grants).
findings.impact: A partner reading its export table sees settlement rows belonging to every tenant that uses it — payout amounts, references, settlement timestamps, customer names, customer emails and destination accounts — with no database-level isolation behind the query that produced it. The isolation mechanism exists and is applied to the two folders that stay inside the organisation, and is absent from the only folder an external party reads.
findings.recommendation: Add the pre-hook to the exports folder so the relation carries the same policy as its siblings, and add an explicit tenant predicate to the model so a run produces one tenant's rows rather than relying on the policy alone. If a partner is genuinely multi-tenant, make the tenant an explicit second variable and materialise one relation per tenant-partner pair.

triage.reason: The compensating control is precisely what is missing here: `enable_row_security` is invoked for staging and marts in dbt_project.yml and not for exports, so no policy exists on this relation to be skipped or not.
The `partner_id` filter at partner_extract.sql:30 narrows by partner and not by tenant; `max_rows` at :58 caps the row count, which bounds volume rather than scope.
The exported columns include customer name, customer email and destination account (partner_extract.sql:52-54), and the recipient is external per the comment at :13.

scope.established_by: Compared the three model folders' hook and grant declarations key by key in dbt_project.yml, then read the export model's predicates.

findings.title: The masked customer model emits raw email, phone and bank account on its full-rebuild branch
findings.class: CWE-359 exposure of private information (privacy: masking not applied)
findings.evidence: The incremental branch masks all three columns — `masked_email("email")` at customer_pii_masked.sql:25, `masked_phone("phone")` at :26 and `masked_account("bank_account")` at :27. The `{% else %}` branch, which dbt takes on any full build, selects the same three columns straight from the source with no macro at all: `email` at :44, `phone` at :45, `bank_account` at :46. The source is `ref("dim_customer")` (:15), which dim_customer.sql:33-36 carries in the clear. The comment at customer_pii_masked.sql:37-39 states this branch runs on the first build of a new environment and whenever the masking policy version changes.
findings.impact: The table every downstream consumer is pointed at contains unmasked contact details and bank account numbers after any full refresh — including the first build in production and any `dbt run --full-refresh`. It is not confined to the warehouse: partner_extract.sql:41 reads this model and ships `email` and `bank_account` to an external partner as `customer_email` and `destination_account`, so a full rebuild publishes raw customer bank accounts to a third party. The state persists until the next incremental run overwrites those rows, and for a customer whose `updated_at` never advances it persists indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same three macros in both branches — the full-rebuild branch should differ only in its `where` clause, never in its projection. Better, define the projection once in a macro or a shared CTE so the two branches cannot diverge, and add a dbt test asserting that `email` matches the masked shape so a regression fails the run.

triage.reason: No compensating layer masks it later: the exports folder in dbt_project.yml carries only `apply_grants` as a post-hook and no masking, and partner_extract.sql:38-41 selects the columns as-is.
This is the branch that ships first. `is_incremental()` is false on the initial build of any environment, so the very first materialisation in production takes the unmasked path.
schema.yml:29-31 identifies the columns as raw contact email and raw destination account, and dim_customer.sql:8-10 calls them the system-of-record contact details.
Nothing narrows the branch: the `{% else %}` at customer_pii_masked.sql:35 has no additional condition and applies to every non-incremental run.

scope.established_by: Diffed the two branches of the same model column by column; three of nine columns are masked on one branch and unmasked on the other.

findings.title: The staging model denormalises raw PII and the folder grant exposes it to every analyst
findings.class: CWE-284 improper access control over personal data
findings.evidence: stg_payout_events.sql:66-69 carries `a.bank_account_number`, `c.display_name`, `c.email` and `c.phone` into the model, joined in from the settlement and CRM sources at :40 and :51. dbt_project.yml grants the staging folder to two roles — `select: ["loader_role", "analyst_role"]` — and `apply_grants` additionally grants the target's reader role on every relation (apply_grants.sql:20-21). The same `analyst_role` also holds the marts grant, and dim_customer.sql:33-36 keeps raw email, phone, bank account and billing address there as a materialised table.
findings.impact: The masking layer is bypassed entirely for anyone holding `analyst_role`: the raw values are available in two separate models without going near `customer_pii_masked`. The architecture's own statement of intent — dim_customer.sql:9-10, 'anything that leaves the analytics schema reads customer_pii_masked instead' — is not enforced by any grant, and the staging copy additionally puts bank account numbers in a schema whose stated purpose is intermediate transformation.
findings.recommendation: Stop carrying the raw columns into staging: join for `customer_id` and let the masked mart supply anything customer-identifying, or mask at the staging boundary. Restrict the raw-bearing relations to a dedicated role that no analyst holds, and make the masked mart the only relation the broad reader roles are granted.

triage.reason: No row- or column-level control compensates: the row-security policy created at row_security.sql:22-24 filters by tenant, not by column, and grants are applied unconditionally by apply_grants.sql:20-21.

PRV-01 decides this and the project itself does: schema.yml:29-31 labels the equivalent columns raw contact email and raw destination account, and the source is the CRM customers table (schema.yml:4-8).
The folder grants are the narrowing that exists, and they name `analyst_role` explicitly, which is the broad population at issue rather than a restriction on it.

scope.established_by: Listed every column of every model that resolves to a CRM or settlement personal-data field, then joined each model to the grants its folder receives in dbt_project.yml.

findings.title: The library that encrypts the stored session token is pinned to an alpha pre-release
findings.class: CWE-1104 pre-release component on a security-critical path
findings.evidence: build.gradle.kts:75 pins the security-crypto artifact to an alpha version. Reachability is established rather than assumed: SessionStore.kt:5-6 imports the encrypted-preferences and master-key types, SessionStore.kt:23-25 builds the master key and SessionStore.kt:27-32 creates the encrypted store that holds the bearer written at :41 and read by AuthInterceptor.kt:23. Every other coordinate in the dependency block is a stable release.
findings.impact: An alpha artifact carries no API or behavioural stability guarantee from its publisher and is not covered by the stable line's support commitments. It is the single most security-critical dependency in the module — what stands between a rooted-device extraction and the technician's session token, which is the property the class comment claims. No CVE is asserted here: this pass is offline with no advisory database, so the pre-release status is reported, which the tree establishes, and not a vulnerability, which it does not.
findings.recommendation: Move to the stable line, or record an explicit decision to stay on the pre-release with an owner and a review date. Either way, check this coordinate against an advisory database in an online run — the one question this pass could not answer.

triage.reason: Not development-only: it is declared as an implementation dependency and is called from the main source set, present in every variant.
The reached sink is the cryptographic API itself, not a peripheral utility of the package.

This bounds the severity to medium. The tree establishes that the artifact is a pre-release and that it is reachable; it cannot establish offline that any specific defect in it is exploitable, so the finding is written down with its reachability evidence and its severity capped.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all eight dependency coordinates and checked each version string for a pre-release qualifier; one hit, whose reachability was then confirmed by import and call-site search.

findings.title: Unknown feature flags default to enabled, so the crew-administration gate opens before the first refresh
findings.class: CWE-1188 insecure default / fail-open authorization (MASVS-AUTH-1)
findings.evidence: FeatureGates.kt:29 returns `snapshot[name] ?: true` — absent means on. The snapshot is empty at process start and is emptied again by `clear()` (FeatureGates.kt:22) and by the `snapshot.clear()` inside `update` (FeatureGates.kt:16) before repopulation. `canManageCrews()` (FeatureGates.kt:32) is built on it and is the only gate on the crew-administration surface: DeepLinkRouter.kt:77 opens `CrewAdminActivity` when it returns true. The author knew the safe form — `demoMode()` on line 38 reads `snapshot["demo_mode"] ?: false`.
findings.impact: Between app start and the first successful flag refresh, and in any window where the server omits `crew_admin` from the payload, any technician who sends `atlas://crew` reaches the crew-administration screen. The server does not compensate: in fieldops-api the role gate `requireRole` is defined at auth.ts:81 and has no call site, so no endpoint enforces a role.
findings.recommendation: Default to false for every flag and require an explicit true, matching `demoMode`. A client-side gate is a user-experience affordance in any case — the authorisation for crew administration has to be enforced on the server, which at present it is not.

triage.reason: The server-side equivalent is absent, and that is established in this tree rather than assumed: fieldops-api/src/middleware/auth.ts:81 defines the role gate and a symbol census across that component finds no call site.
The flag map is populated from the API response at FeatureGates.kt:14-20, and the failure mode under discussion is its absence rather than its content.
It is not defence in depth with a working equivalent elsewhere; it is the only check on the path at DeepLinkRouter.kt:77.

scope.established_by: Compared the two accessor idioms in the same object — one defaults true, one defaults false — and traced the true-defaulting one to its authorization use.

findings.title: The attachment uploader attaches the session bearer to a server-supplied URL on a redirect-following client
findings.class: CWE-200 credential transmitted to an unintended host (MASVS-NETWORK-1)
findings.evidence: AuthInterceptor exists to prevent exactly this: its doc comment at AuthInterceptor.kt:9-12 states that presigned URLs point at storage hosts the app does not control 'so the token must not follow them', and it enforces that with a host equality check at AuthInterceptor.kt:19. `AttachmentUploader.upload` bypasses the interceptor and sets the header by hand — AttachmentSync.kt:80 `.header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")` — on a request whose URL is the `uploadUrl` parameter, which the class docstring (AttachmentSync.kt:66-68) describes as coming back from the API. It sends it on `ApiClient.uploads`, which is configured with `followRedirects(true)` at ApiClient.kt:62 and carries no AuthInterceptor.
findings.impact: The session bearer is transmitted to whatever host the API names, and then onward to any host that storage redirects to. The invariant the interceptor was written to hold is broken by the one call site that does not use it, so the protection reads as present while the credential-bearing path goes around it.
findings.recommendation: Do not send the session bearer to a URL the app did not construct. Use the presigned URL as issued, with no Authorization header, and if the storage host needs authentication have the API return a scoped credential for it. Set `followRedirects(false)` on the uploads client regardless.

triage.reason: The compensating control is the interceptor's host check at AuthInterceptor.kt:19, and this path does not reach it: the interceptor is installed on the `api` client (ApiClient.kt:49) and this request is made on `uploads` (AttachmentSync.kt:85).
`uploadUrl` is a parameter fed from an API response per AttachmentSync.kt:66-68, not a constant or a value bounded by an allowlist.
Nothing narrows the destination — there is no scheme or host check anywhere in `upload` (AttachmentSync.kt:72-88).

scope.established_by: Enumerated every place an Authorization header is set: one interceptor with a host check, one manual call site with none.

findings.title: Every Python dependency is declared with an open-ended lower bound and no ceiling
findings.class: CWE-1104 use of unmaintained or uncontrolled third-party components
findings.evidence: The two Python manifests declare eleven dependencies between them and not one carries an upper bound — atlas-rag/pyproject.toml:7-12 and settlement-worker/pyproject.toml:7-11. The npm side at least caps the major version through caret ranges.
findings.impact: A resolve accepts any future major version, including one with different security semantics: the model client admits a new major whose authentication and request handling differ, and the validation library admits a new major whose behaviour would silently change what the payout model accepts. With no lock, nothing bounds this at install time either, so the two defects compound.
findings.recommendation: Add upper bounds on the major for every direct dependency so a breaking major is an explicit decision, and back that with a committed hash-pinned lock. Do not blanket-upgrade to latest as a remediation.

triage.reason: The exculpation is a committed lock plus a deterministic install command; neither exists anywhere in the tree.
This does not reduce to an informational note about the manifest, which is what would apply if a lock pinned the actual resolution. With nothing pinning it, the manifest is the resolution.
These are runtime dependencies, not development or test extras; they install into the deployed environment that runs the console entry points.

scope.established_by: Enumerated both dependency arrays line by line and checked each specifier for an upper bound; all eleven lack one.

findings.title: Key exchange and key rotation accept a credential in the body with no rate limit
findings.class: CWE-307 improper restriction of authentication attempts
findings.evidence: `/v1/query` is throttled at app.py:144 through `limits.allow`. `/v1/token` (app.py:204-219) and `/v1/keys/rotate` (app.py:222-242) each call `_principal_for_key` on a body field — app.py:208 and app.py:226 — and neither consults `limits.allow`; a grep for `limits.allow` in the module returns one occurrence. Both endpoints distinguish a valid key from an invalid one by status code, so each is an oracle.
findings.impact: Unlimited offline-speed guessing against the API key space, and unlimited issuance of session tokens for any key that is guessed or stolen. Rotation is worse than exchange: app.py:233 revokes the presented key and app.py:237 issues a replacement, so an attacker holding a stolen key locks the legitimate owner out while retaining access.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same limiter to every endpoint that evaluates a credential, keyed by source address rather than by tenant since the tenant is not known until the credential is validated. Require an authenticated session, not merely possession of the old key, before rotating it.

triage.reason: No other throttle exists in the service; limits.py exports one `allow` function with one call site.
The guard's scope is narrower than the credential surface: it covers one of the three routes that evaluate a key.

A gateway or WAF in front of the service could throttle these paths; the component ships no deployment artifact and the only proxy in the tree, pulumi-platform/edge.ts, does not route to this service. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS.

scope.established_by: Listed every route that evaluates a credential and joined it against every call to the rate limiter.

findings.title: The public playground key can mint a persistent private API key through the rotation endpoint
findings.class: CWE-269 improper privilege management
findings.evidence: `_principal_for_key` resolves the documented sandbox key to a real principal before any database lookup: app.py:56-57 returns `Principal(settings.demo_tenant, 'playground', frozenset({'public'}))` when the presented key equals `settings.demo_api_key`, which settings.py:46-47 records as printed in the documentation. `rotate_key` accepts that principal at app.py:226-228 and then inserts a fresh row into `rag.api_keys` bound to its tenant and subject (app.py:237-241). The demo key is not a row in that table, so the revoke at app.py:233 matches nothing and the demo key keeps working alongside the new one.
findings.impact: Anyone who reads the public documentation obtains a durable, individually issued API key for the demo tenant that is indistinguishable from a real credential in the keys table, and does so as many times as they like. It converts a deliberately public, revocable-by-code-change value into unbounded rows of issued credentials, and it defeats any counting or auditing of who holds a key.
findings.recommendation: Reject the demo principal explicitly on `/v1/keys/rotate` and `/v1/token`, or better, make the sandbox key an ordinary row in `rag.api_keys` with a flag that bars it from credential-management endpoints, so the special case disappears from the authentication path.

triage.reason: No check distinguishes the demo principal downstream: app.py:226-241 branches only on the principal being non-None.

The key's exposure is intended and bounded to the public FAQ by retriever.py:39-41 — but issuing new credentials from it is not part of that intent, and FP-05 requires the finding to move to what the intended exposure enables, which is what is reported here.
The artefact created is a credential row, not public content.

scope.established_by: Traced the demo short-circuit in the principal resolver into each endpoint that consumes a principal, and read what the rotation endpoint writes.

findings.title: The ingest retry path re-persists the stored raw text without the redaction both live paths apply
findings.class: CWE-359 exposure of private information (LLM02:2025)
findings.evidence: Both live ingestion paths wrap the text: `ingest_document` calls `redact(doc.text)` at ingest.py:85 and `consume_manifest` calls `redact(entry['text'])` at ingest.py:102. `retry_failed` does not — ingest.py:130-136 passes `row['raw_text']` straight into `_persist_chunks`, and `_failed_rows` selects that column verbatim at ingest.py:110. `redact` (ingest.py:41-44) is what removes card numbers, account identifiers and national identifiers per the comment at ingest.py:24.
findings.impact: A document that failed mid-ingest and is later retried lands in the chunk table with the payment and identity numbers the redaction exists to strip, and those chunks are then sent to the third-party embedding provider by `_persist_chunks` through embedder.embed (ingest.py:60). The failure path produces exactly the data the success path is careful to avoid, and does so silently.
findings.recommendation: Call `redact` in `retry_failed` as the other two paths do, or better, move the call inside `_persist_chunks` so every writer inherits it and a fourth path cannot be added without it. Re-examine any chunks already written by this path.

triage.reason: `retry_failed` has no caller in the component — a grep returns only its definition at ingest.py:126 — and it is not exposed as a route or a console script (pyproject.toml:14-15 declares only `atlas-rag`). Its trigger, presumably an operator or a scheduler, is outside what is in scope, which caps this at probable.
No redaction happens downstream: `_persist_chunks` (ingest.py:52-78) splits, embeds and inserts without inspecting the text.
The comment at ingest.py:24 identifies the values as card numbers, bank accounts and national identifiers, and the patterns at ingest.py:26-28 confirm it.

scope.established_by: Grouped the three callers of `_persist_chunks` and diffed how each prepares its text argument; two redact, one does not.

findings.title: The replay cache is an unbounded in-process dictionary keyed by an attacker-supplied header
findings.class: CWE-770 allocation without limits
findings.evidence: limits.py:16 declares a module-level dict written by `remember_response` at limits.py:52 with no size bound and no eviction: an entry is removed only when the same key is read back after expiry (limits.py:45-46). The key is `replay:` plus the client's `Idempotency-Key` header, taken unvalidated at app.py:153 — the header is not in QUERY_SCHEMA and is subject to no length or format constraint. Each stored value is a full answer payload including the generated text.
findings.impact: A caller issues requests with a fresh random `Idempotency-Key` each time and every one permanently retains an answer payload in the process heap until restart. This is a cheaper denial of service than the model calls themselves, because the retained memory outlives the request, and the rate limiter at app.py:144 caps requests per minute but not lifetime accumulation.
findings.recommendation: Bound the cache with a maximum entry count and evict least-recently-used, sweep expired entries on a timer rather than only on access, and constrain the accepted key to a bounded character set and length before it becomes a dictionary key.

triage.reason: The key is a request header read at app.py:153 with no validation; QUERY_SCHEMA (app.py:21-31) governs the body only.
The per-minute limiter bounds request rate, not retained entries — an attacker within the limit still accumulates 60 payloads a minute indefinitely.
Caching replies is intended, but the module docstring's stated bound — that the cache 'only has to survive a client retry' (limits.py:5) — is not implemented anywhere in the file.

scope.established_by: Traced the dictionary's writes and deletes, then traced the key back to the unvalidated request header.

findings.title: Tool arguments from the model are splatted as keyword arguments with no schema validation
findings.class: CWE-20 improper input validation (LLM06:2025)
findings.evidence: tools.py:104 parses the model's raw argument string with `json.loads` and tools.py:109 calls `await fn(principal, **arguments)`. The declared parameter schemas in TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:70-74, 82-87) — including their `required` lists and property types — are sent to the model but never enforced on the way back. `jsonschema` is a declared dependency of this project (pyproject.toml:12) and is imported and used in app.py:11 for request bodies, so the validation idiom exists in the codebase and is simply absent here.
findings.impact: The model's output, which an injected document influences, decides the keyword arguments of a Python call. Today the reachable effect is a crash — an unexpected key raises TypeError inside the request handler — but the guarantee that a tool receives only its declared parameters, of the declared types, does not exist. Any future tool with an optional parameter that widens its behaviour is directly settable from model output.
findings.recommendation: Validate `arguments` against the tool's own JSON Schema from TOOL_SPECS before dispatch, reject on mismatch and return a structured error to the model rather than raising, and pass parameters explicitly instead of splatting.

triage.reason: No validation layer sits between: tools.py:99-109 is the whole path from tool name to call, and its only check is that the name is a registry key.
The sink is a Python call with caller-controlled keyword names, not a parser.

Bounded to medium: with the two tools currently registered, the worst directly reachable outcome is an unhandled TypeError rather than a behaviour change, because neither tool has an optional parameter that widens what it does. The finding is written down because the missing enforcement, not the current tool list, is the defect.

scope.established_by: Compared the request-body validation idiom in app.py with the tool-argument path; the former validates against a schema, the latter splats.

findings.title: No lockfile exists for any of the four dependency manifests
findings.class: CWE-1357 reliance on un-pinned components
findings.evidence: A search over the whole target root for every ecosystem's lock filename returns nothing. Both npm manifests declare only caret ranges and neither declares a package-manager field, so the resolver itself is unpinned. Neither Python project declares a build-system table, so installation falls back to a legacy backend, and no hash-pinned input exists for either service.
findings.impact: Every install re-resolves against the live registries. Two installs a day apart produce different trees, an audit result describes versions that may never be deployed, and a compromised patch release of any direct or transitive dependency is picked up automatically with no review. It also removes the integrity hashes that would detect a substituted artifact.
findings.recommendation: Commit lockfiles for both npm projects and install with the clean-install command and scripts disabled. For the Python services generate and commit a hash-pinned lock and install requiring hashes. Add a package-manager field and a build-system table so the resolver and backend are declared rather than inferred.

triage.reason: The library exculpation does not apply: both package manifests set private true and both Python projects describe deployed services. These are applications, where the lock is committed by design.
The exculpation would be a lock plus a deterministic install in a pipeline. Neither exists — no lock, and no CI workflow, Dockerfile or pipeline file anywhere under the target root.

An internal proxy or registry mirror freezing versions would bound this, and there is no evidence either way: no registry configuration exists in the tree. Per FP-08 this cannot be HOLDS, and it caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every dependency-declaring manifest in the tree, then searched the whole target root for each ecosystem's lock filename; zero hits.

findings.title: The role gate is implemented and never applied to any route
findings.class: CWE-1188 control present but not wired (A01:2021)
findings.evidence: auth.ts:81-89 exports `requireRole(...roles)`, a middleware returning 403 unless the actor's role matches. A grep for the symbol across src/ returns exactly one occurrence: the definition itself. No route module imports it; index.ts imports only `attachActor` and `requireAuth` (index.ts:6). The `Role` type distinguishes four levels (auth.ts:5) and `policy.ts` branches on all of them, so the distinction is meant to be load-bearing.
findings.impact: Function-level authorization does not exist on this API. Every authenticated caller, whatever their role, reaches every route: creating and updating work orders, uploading attachments and printing sheets. The presence of a role gate in the codebase makes reviewers believe otherwise, which is why the missing checks on individual handlers were not noticed.
findings.recommendation: Apply it where the role distinction is meant to hold, then add a test that a `tech` receives 403 from a manager-only route — the gate is currently unfalsifiable because nothing exercises it.

triage.reason: The scope is the whole service: ten source files, all read, and no route registration lives outside index.ts.

It is an ordinary exported factory used by explicit import in Hono, not a decorator or convention-registered hook; the sibling middlewares in the same file are imported by name at index.ts:6, so a symbol search is a valid census.
There is no other layer performing role checks: the only authorization functions in the tree are in policy.ts and are called from two handlers only.

scope.established_by: Symbol census across src/ for `requireRole`: one definition, zero call sites, against `requireAuth` which has one definition and one mount.

findings.title: Attachment upload buffers the entire request body into memory with no size limit
findings.class: CWE-770 allocation without limits (A04:2021)
findings.evidence: attachments.ts:40 parses the multipart body and attachments.ts:53 does `Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer())`, materialising the whole upload in the process heap before attachments.ts:54 writes it. No limit is applied anywhere: there is no body-size middleware in index.ts, no check on `file.size` before the read, and `bytes` is only recorded afterwards at attachments.ts:62. There is also no allowlist on `file.type`, which is stored as given.
findings.impact: A single authenticated request with a multi-gigabyte body exhausts the container's memory and terminates the process; concurrent requests do so faster. The API runs one task per availability zone by its own account (rateLimit.ts:6-7), so the blast radius of one such request is a whole zone's capacity.
findings.recommendation: Impose a maximum body size at the server boundary and reject earlier requests by `Content-Length`, then stream the body to disk rather than buffering it. Validate the declared content type against an allowlist before storing it.

triage.reason: No size control exists in the tree: index.ts registers only `logger` and `secureHeaders` globally (index.ts:15-16), neither of which bounds a body.
Accepting uploads is intended, but nothing bounds the size — which is what FP-05 requires to exculpate.

A load balancer or proxy body-size cap would bound this; pulumi-platform/edge.ts declares listeners and rules but no request-size limit, and no other proxy artifact is in scope. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, which is why this is reported as a resource issue and not as a confirmed outage path.

scope.established_by: Traced the upload from `formData()` to the heap allocation and checked every middleware registered in index.ts for a size bound.

findings.title: Attachment upload does not verify that the target work order belongs to the caller's organisation
findings.class: CWE-639 authorization bypass through user-controlled key (API1:2023)
findings.evidence: attachments.ts:42 takes `workOrderId` verbatim from the submitted form and attachments.ts:56-62 inserts the row with that value and the caller's own `org_id`. No query verifies that the work order exists or that its `org_id` matches — contrast the update handler in workorders.ts:117-123, which loads the row and compares the organisation before writing.
findings.impact: An authenticated user attaches arbitrary files to any work-order identifier, including identifiers belonging to other organisations. Because the stored `org_id` is the uploader's, the record is inconsistent with the work order it claims to belong to: any consumer that lists attachments by work order without re-checking the organisation surfaces an outsider's file inside another tenant's record.
findings.recommendation: Look up the work order by id and organisation before inserting, exactly as the update handler does, and reject when it does not resolve.

triage.reason: No foreign-key or trigger evidence exists in the tree — there is no migration or DDL anywhere in fieldops-api — and no code path re-validates the pair.
`workOrderId` is read from the multipart form at attachments.ts:42 with only a non-empty check at attachments.ts:44.
Storing the caller's `org_id` at attachments.ts:62 looks like a narrowing but constrains the new row only, not the work order it points at.

scope.established_by: Compared the write handlers that accept a foreign identifier: the work-order updater resolves and checks it, the attachment uploader does not.

findings.title: Refresh tokens are stored and matched in plaintext with no rotation or single-use
findings.class: CWE-522 insufficiently protected credentials
findings.evidence: session.ts:102 matches `r.token = $1` against the value supplied by the client, so the column holds the token verbatim rather than a digest — contrast the password column, which session.ts:39-46 stores as `scrypt$salt$key`. The row is not deleted or rotated after use (no delete or update follows at session.ts:105-107), and no single-use marker is checked, so one refresh token mints unlimited session tokens until `expires_at`.
findings.impact: Anyone who reads the refresh_tokens table — through a database backup, a read-only reporting connection, or the shared analytics replica that pulumi-platform/data.ts:64 exposes to the internet — obtains directly usable credentials for every principal with an active refresh token. Replay is unlimited and leaves no distinguishing trace.
findings.recommendation: Store `digest(token)` and match on the digest; issue a new refresh token on every exchange and invalidate the presented one, so a replayed token is detectable and a stolen one is short-lived.

triage.reason: The stored value is the credential itself, not a placeholder; session.ts:103 passes the client-supplied string straight into the comparison.
No compensating control binds the token to a device or client: the query's only other predicate is the expiry at session.ts:102.
The data is an authentication credential; its exposure yields sessions for arbitrary principals.

scope.established_by: Compared the storage form of the two credential types in the same file: passwords are hashed with a scheme prefix, refresh tokens are compared as literals.

findings.title: The read replica omits the parameter group, so the primary's forced TLS does not apply to it
findings.class: CWE-319 cleartext transmission
findings.evidence: data.ts:26-32 declares a parameter group forcing TLS and data.ts:42 attaches it to the primary only. The replica declaration at data.ts:59-67 sets the source, class, subnet group, groups, public accessibility, encryption and snapshot behaviour, but no parameter group — an omitted argument, so the replica takes the engine default where forced TLS is off. Backup retention and deletion protection are omitted on the replica for the same reason.
findings.impact: The replica accepts plaintext database sessions. Combined with its public address and open port, production data replicated to it is readable on the wire and credentials are presented over an unencrypted channel to an internet-facing endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Pass the parameter group on the replica declaration, and set backup retention and deletion protection there as they are set on the primary.

triage.reason: No other layer forces TLS for the replica: the only forced-TLS declaration in the tree is bound to the primary.
The sink is a live database listener reached over the internet, not a parsed or inert format.
It is not a defence-in-depth extra: with no server-side enforcement a misconfigured client silently negotiates plaintext and nothing rejects it.

scope.established_by: Compared the primary's argument list against the replica's argument by argument; three arguments appear only on the primary.

findings.title: The reports distribution uses the default certificate, pinning the viewer security policy to an obsolete TLS version
findings.class: CWE-326 inadequate encryption strength
findings.evidence: edge.ts:255 sets the viewer certificate to the provider default with no minimum protocol version and no ACM certificate — an omitted argument. With the default certificate the oldest security policy applies and the minimum version cannot be raised. The load balancer alongside it sets a modern policy at edge.ts:82, and the stack already holds an ACM certificate ARN used for the ALB only.
findings.impact: Rendered customer reports are served over a distribution that negotiates obsolete TLS versions, below the baseline the ALB on the same stack already meets, and the customer-facing URL carries no organisation-controlled certificate.
findings.recommendation: Attach the ACM certificate the stack already requires, with SNI and a modern minimum protocol version, and add the corresponding aliases. Add distribution logging at the same time.

triage.reason: The sink is the live viewer TLS negotiation on the distribution that serves the reports bucket origin.
Nothing in front of the distribution can raise its TLS floor; the web ACL inspects paths, not protocol versions.
It is load-bearing rather than defence in depth: it is the transport protecting customer report content and no second encrypted channel is declared.

scope.established_by: Read the distribution's argument list key by key; minimum protocol version, aliases and logging are all absent.

findings.title: Task-role grants use wildcard bucket and account ARNs, and the per-tenant policy cannot narrow them
findings.class: CWE-732 resource not scoped to account or tenant
findings.evidence: iam.ts:39 grants object and list actions on wildcard export bucket ARNs; iam.ts:20 and :32 do the same on wildcard report bucket ARNs; iam.ts:25 grants secret reads with both region and account wildcarded. index.ts:72-84 then attaches a second role policy scoping reads to a per-tenant prefix.
findings.impact: Bucket names are a global namespace and none of these ARNs pins an account, so the roles may read and write buckets outside this stack, this tenant and this account — an outbound exfiltration channel for a compromised task and a cross-tenant read path for the loader. The narrowing added in index.ts is inert: IAM unions Allow statements, so an extra Allow can only widen.
findings.recommendation: Build the ARNs from the actual bucket outputs and pass them into the role factory instead of literal wildcards, and pin the account in the secret ARN. If a wildcard must stay, add a resource-account condition to each statement.

triage.reason: No service control policy, permissions boundary or resource-account condition exists in the tree.
The per-tenant block looks like a narrowing but is a separate Allow on the same role, which cannot subtract; there is no Deny and no Condition in either block.
The alternative reading — that auto-naming suffixes make the wildcard match fewer buckets — makes the grants sloppier rather than narrower; the pattern is still unbounded across accounts.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every Resource value in the policy record and every role policy attached to those roles across the tree.

findings.title: The reports bucket policy grants the partner role the whole bucket, bypassing the edge rule that blocks the staff-only prefix
findings.class: CWE-284 improper access control / edge control bypassed at the origin
findings.evidence: edge.ts:205-206 and :216-233 declare a web ACL rule blocking any request whose path begins with the internal prefix on the reports distribution. storage.ts:114-132 grants the partner analytics role object and list actions on the bucket ARN and everything under it at storage.ts:127 — prefix-unqualified — and storage.ts:111-113 states the partner reads the bucket directly rather than through the distribution.
findings.impact: The only control protecting staff-only working material is enforced at the edge, and the third party is granted a path around it. The partner, or anyone who obtains that role, lists and downloads every object in the bucket including the prefix the design treats as internal.
findings.recommendation: Scope the resource to the partner's prefix and add a list condition restricting the prefix, plus an explicit Deny on the internal prefix for principals other than the renderer role.

triage.reason: The statement contains no condition and no prefix restriction; the list grant is on the bare bucket ARN.
The control that exists is bound to the distribution and cannot see a direct object read, and the code states the direct path is the intended one.
The bucket is tagged as holding rendered customer reports and the internal prefix is described as staff-only working material.

scope.established_by: Joined the bucket's only policy to its two consumers: the distribution origin and the partner role ARN.

findings.title: Two bucket policies target the same exports bucket in staging, so which grant is live is undefined
findings.class: CWE-732 conflicting declarations of one access control
findings.evidence: With both staging flags enabled, storage.ts:50-68 and storage.ts:70-89 each create a bucket policy resource for the same bucket id at storage.ts:52 and :74. S3 holds exactly one policy document per bucket, so each resource issues its own write, the later replaces the earlier, and every subsequent refresh shows one of the two as drifted.
findings.impact: Neither grant is reliable. If the public policy wins, anonymous read of production-replicated exports is live; if the replication policy wins, the public policy silently disappears and reappears between deployments. An access-control outcome that flips between runs cannot be audited, and the drift will be dismissed as noise.
findings.recommendation: Build one policy document with both statements and attach a single policy resource, or move the replication grant into the source account's replication role rather than a destination bucket policy.

triage.reason: They are not two different buckets: both pass the same bucket id from storage.ts:28.
Both branches are taken in the shipped staging configuration; this is not a debug-only path.
The finding is about two constructs colliding, not about one construct's scope.

scope.established_by: Counted bucket policy resources per bucket id; only the exports bucket receives two, and only when both config flags are true.
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 sets both flags false, so the production stack creates neither policy and does not collide.

findings.title: The assets bucket publishes the web bundle over a plaintext website endpoint with no public access block
findings.class: CWE-319 / CWE-668 plaintext distribution channel
findings.evidence: storage.ts:136-143 creates the bucket and a website configuration on it. Unlike its two siblings this bucket receives no public access block, no server-side encryption configuration and no versioning, and no distribution in the tree points at it — the only distribution's origin is the reports bucket. An S3 website endpoint speaks plaintext HTTP only. The staging stack records that the payments publishable key is embedded in this bundle.
findings.impact: The published web bundle, including the booking widget that handles payments, is served over unauthenticated plaintext with no integrity protection, so a network position between the customer and storage yields script injection into a payments flow. The missing public access block also leaves this the one bucket whose exposure is decided outside the code.
findings.recommendation: Put a distribution with an origin access control in front of the bucket — the pattern already used for reports — remove the website configuration, and add an explicit public access block with all four flags true plus an encryption configuration, matching the sibling buckets.

triage.reason: For confidentiality the bundle is public by design, but the surviving issue is integrity and transport, and the bundle is the payments booking widget per the staging stack config.
Public serving is intended but nothing bounds it to a TLS path: the only serving mechanism declared for this bucket is the plaintext website endpoint.
A CDN or account-level public access block may exist outside the repository; no exported artifact accompanies these files, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS.

scope.established_by: Compared the three buckets' companion resources one by one and searched the tree for any distribution referencing this bucket; none exists.

findings.title: Every operational field travels through logging extras that the configured formatter discards
findings.class: CWE-778 insufficient logging
findings.evidence: consumer.py:122 configures logging with a level and no format, so the basic format applies and renders no extra attributes. Every diagnostic field in the package travels in `extra`: consumer.py:96 (entry id, type, result), consumer.py:91 and :115 (the id of the failed entry), handlers.py:39 and :83, retry.py:39 and :45. Executing the same formatter over the same call shape emits the message text alone with no id, type or result. `structlog` is declared at pyproject.toml:11 and imported by no module, so the structured pipeline that would render these fields does not exist here.
findings.impact: A money-moving worker produces an untraceable log. After an incident there is no way to join a ledger movement to the stream entry that caused it, no record of which entry was dead-lettered, and no record of which dead letter the drain job replayed — the path with no signature and no authorization check. It also removes detection as a compensating control for every other finding in this component.
findings.recommendation: Either adopt the declared structured logger and its renderer, or configure a formatter that includes the extra fields, and assert at startup that the entry id, message type and idempotency key appear in the emitted record. Log dead-letter reasons and replays as security-relevant events.

triage.reason: If a deployment configures the root logger before main runs, the basic configuration call returns early and a structured formatter could render the fields; no deployment or logging config was in scope. That caps this at probable.
This is the absence arm of the procedure, not a disclosure claim; the sink drops the data rather than exposing it.
No other audit record exists: the journal stores the movement but carries no stream entry id, actor or message type.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all logging calls with the escaper tool, then checked each extra key against the formatter the configuration installs; confirmed by executing that formatter.

findings.title: Settlement receipts are posted in cleartext to a redirect-following client with no egress control
findings.class: CWE-319 cleartext transmission of sensitive information
findings.evidence: handlers.py:73 posts the receipt built at handlers.py:65-72 — tenant, destination account, amount, currency and resulting balance — to the configured notification URL, which settings.py:46 defaults to a plaintext http scheme. handlers.py:37 sends it with redirects enabled and no allowlist, no proxy and no scheme check. On a 307 or 308 the method and body are preserved, so the notification host, or anyone able to answer for that plaintext hostname on the internal segment, redirects the settlement data to a host of its choosing.
findings.impact: Per-payout financial data crosses the internal network unencrypted and unauthenticated in both directions, and the destination is one redirect away from being attacker-chosen.
findings.recommendation: Use TLS with certificate verification, disable redirect following on a webhook, and validate the resolved address against an allowlist before the request. Send an opaque settlement identifier rather than the amount and balance.

triage.reason: For the request-forgery reading only: the hook URL is a configuration constant at settings.py:45-47 and the sole call site passes no message field, so forgery from the message is ruled out and recorded in ruled_out.
For the cleartext and redirect claim: no proxy, allowlist or scheme check exists anywhere in the package; handlers.py:37 is the only outbound call.
The body carries account identifiers, amounts and post-settlement balances.
A service mesh terminating TLS or an egress policy would bound this and no infrastructure artifact for this component was in scope; hence probable.

scope.established_by: Enumerated outbound HTTP sinks: one sink, one call site, one URL source.
scope.narrowed_by: Only 307 and 308 redirects preserve the body; other codes convert to GET and drop it.

findings.title: Idempotency slots are global rather than tenant-scoped, so one tenant's key suppresses another's settlement
findings.class: CWE-639 authorization bypass through user-controlled key
findings.evidence: idempotency.py:26 builds the key from a constant prefix and the idempotency key alone, with no tenant component — while ledger.py:36 correctly namespaces balance keys by tenant. Callers pass only the message's idempotency key (handlers.py:81, 87, 110). The key itself carries no uniqueness requirement beyond a length constraint at schemas.py:26, and on the consume path even that is unenforced.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant collision, accidental or deliberate. An attacker who can guess another tenant's key formats pre-seeds slots to suppress that tenant's payouts, each of which then reports as settled without any money having moved, and the cached receipt handed back belongs to the other tenant.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant in the slot and require the key to be tenant-unique at the producer. Compare the cached receipt's tenant against the message before replaying it.

triage.reason: Nothing narrows the key: the prefix is a constant and no caller adds a tenant component.
The idempotency key is a free-form message field.
The cached value is a settlement receipt carrying tenant, destination account, amount and resulting balance.

scope.established_by: Compared the key construction with the tenant-scoped equivalent at ledger.py:36 and listed all three call sites.
scope.narrowed_by: The receipt is cached but not printed under the shipped log formatter, so the impact is settlement suppression rather than disclosure.

findings.title: The bootstrap grants revoke DELETE and TRUNCATE on the journal but leave UPDATE
findings.class: CWE-732 incorrect permission assignment
findings.evidence: ledger.py:20 grants all privileges on every table in the schema to the application role and ledger.py:21-22 takes back DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER. UPDATE is not among them, so the role retains the ability to rewrite any journal row in place — against the stated intent at ledger.py:16-18. Two further gaps in the same four lines: the grant is point-in-time with no default privileges, so tables created later are covered by neither the grant nor the revoke; and the connection string the worker uses defaults to a different role name than the statements name.
findings.impact: A bug, an injected statement or a compromised worker can rewrite settled movements rather than being confined to appending, which destroys audit history as effectively as deleting it. The comment above the block asserts a property the SQL does not create, which is why nobody re-reads it.
findings.recommendation: Add UPDATE to the revoke list, or grant INSERT and SELECT explicitly instead of granting all and subtracting. Add default privileges so later tables inherit the policy, and confirm the runtime role is the one these statements name.

triage.reason: No append-only trigger or rule appears anywhere; this is the only DDL in scope and the revoke explicitly gives back trigger-creation control rather than adding one.
It reads as a hardening block and is one; the defect is which verb is missing, which is decidable in the four lines shown.

The grants name one role while the connection default names another; if the runtime role differs, the block governs less than it appears to. No deployment artifact in scope settles which role runs, hence probable.

scope.established_by: Read the grant and revoke pair verb by verb against the intent stated immediately above it.

findings.title: max_delivery_attempts is declared and read by nothing; the first exception dead-letters and acks the message
findings.class: CWE-1188 / CWE-754 improper check for unusual conditions
findings.evidence: settings.py:51 declares the setting with an environment override and it has zero readers across the package. The only other occurrence of the name is prose — consumer.py:5, the module docstring claiming failures go to the dead-letter stream after that many attempts. The code does the opposite: consumer.py:112-117 catches the first exception of any kind, writes the entry to the dead-letter stream and acks it, so a transient database timeout permanently removes the payout from the authenticated path on attempt one.
findings.impact: There is no retry. Every transient failure moves a payout onto the dead-letter path, which is the path that performs no signature verification and no authorization check. The operator-facing knob makes a bounded retry policy appear to be in force.
findings.recommendation: Either implement it by counting deliveries and dead-lettering only past the threshold, or delete the setting and the docstring claim. Distinguish retryable failures from permanent rejections and never store the latter for replay.

triage.reason: The scope is the whole distribution — nine modules plus the manifest — and no other package exists here for a reader to live in.
It is a plain dataclass attribute read by attribute access elsewhere in the file; its siblings have exactly such readers at consumer.py:105-106 and this one has none.

scope.established_by: Counted readers of every bound-declaring key in settings.py; two siblings have one each, this one has none.

findings.title: The grant macro falls back to the PUBLIC pseudo-role for any target it does not recognise
findings.class: CWE-276 incorrect default permissions
findings.evidence: apply_grants.sql:11-15 maps three target names to reader roles and apply_grants.sql:17 resolves anything else with `reader_by_target.get(target.name, "public")`. The macro then issues `grant usage on schema ... to {{ reader }}` and `grant select on {{ relation }} to {{ reader }}` (apply_grants.sql:20-21). In PostgreSQL `public` is not an ordinary role name — every role is a member of it — so a grant to `public` makes the relation readable by every database user. The macro is the post-hook on all three model folders in dbt_project.yml, so it runs on every relation the project builds.
findings.impact: A run against any target whose name is not exactly `prod`, `ci` or `dev` grants SELECT on every model — including `dim_customer` with raw contact details and `partner_extract` — to every user of the database. Adding a target, renaming one, or invoking `dbt run --target staging` is enough, and the run reports success with the log line at apply_grants.sql:31 naming `public` as the reader.
findings.recommendation: Fail the run instead of guessing: raise a compile error when `target.name` is not in the map, so an unmapped target is a build failure rather than a silent public grant. Never use `public` as a fallback value in a grant statement.

triage.reason: The fallback is a literal in the macro and the value that selects it, `target.name`, comes from the invocation rather than from a fixed constant.

The reachable set is narrower than it looks today: profiles.yml defines exactly the three targets the map covers (dev at :8, ci at :20, prod at :32), so no currently declared target takes the fallback. This is why the severity is medium rather than high; the defect is that the failure mode of adding a fourth is a public grant.
Nothing revokes afterwards: `apply_grants` issues only grants, and the folder-level `+grants` blocks in dbt_project.yml add roles rather than restricting the set.

scope.established_by: Read the lookup's default against the target names declared in profiles.yml, and traced the resolved value into both grant statements.
scope.narrowed_by: warehouse-dbt/profiles.yml:8, :20, :32 — the three declared targets are exactly the three mapped keys, so the fallback is unreachable until a target is added.

findings.title: Every rebuilt relation is granted insert and update to two service roles, including the masked mart and the partner export
findings.class: CWE-732 incorrect permission assignment
findings.evidence: apply_grants.sql:25-26 grants `insert, update` on `{{ relation }}` to `settlement_app` and to `warehouse_loader`, unconditionally, inside the macro that dbt_project.yml declares as the post-hook for the staging, marts and exports folders alike. There is no branch on folder, model name or materialisation, so `customer_pii_masked` and `partner_extract` receive the same write grants as the staging tables the comment at apply_grants.sql:23-24 is actually about.
findings.impact: Two service roles can write to the relation that is supposed to be the masked view of customer data and to the table an external partner reads. A compromised or buggy loader can overwrite masked values with unmasked ones, or alter the amounts and destination accounts in the partner export, and because the grants are reissued on every dbt run any manual revocation is undone at the next build.
findings.recommendation: Scope the write grants to the relations that genuinely receive out-of-band writes — pass the roles in as a per-folder variable, or branch on the model's folder — so marts and exports get read grants only.

triage.reason: No condition narrows the two statements; they are emitted for every relation the macro is called with, and dbt_project.yml calls it for all three folders.
The row-security policy does not compensate: it is `for select` only (row_security.sql:22), so it constrains no write, and the exports folder has no policy at all.
The comment at apply_grants.sql:23-24 states the intent — the loader and settlement service write between runs — but nothing bounds the grant to the relations that intent covers.

scope.established_by: Traced which models the post-hook applies to via dbt_project.yml, then read the statements the macro emits for each.

findings.title: The tenant isolation policy covers only SELECT and is not forced, so writers and the owner are unconstrained
findings.class: CWE-1230 incomplete row-level security
findings.evidence: row_security.sql:22-24 creates `policy tenant_isolation ... for select using (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true))`. Two gaps in four lines. The `for select` clause means INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are governed by no policy, and `apply_grants` hands `insert, update` on every relation to `settlement_app` and `warehouse_loader` (apply_grants.sql:25-26). And `alter table ... enable row level security` at row_security.sql:18 does not apply to the table's owner; PostgreSQL requires `force row level security` for that, and the owner here is the dbt connection user from profiles.yml, which is the same identity the loader roles may share.
findings.impact: Tenant isolation is read-only and owner-exempt. A role with the write grants this project issues can insert or modify rows carrying any tenant's identifier, and any session connected as the table owner reads every tenant's rows despite the policy being present and appearing to enforce. The comment at row_security.sql:4-6 states a session 'can only ever address its own rows', which holds for readers that are not the owner and for no one else.
findings.recommendation: Drop the `for select` restriction so the policy covers all commands, add a `with check` clause so writes cannot set a foreign tenant, and add `alter table {{ relation }} force row level security` so the owner is bound too. Confirm which role dbt connects as and that it is not also the application write role.

triage.reason: No second control exists: the grants macro is the only other server-side statement the project issues and it widens rather than restricts, and no model carries a tenant predicate of its own except through this policy.
The `using` clause narrows which rows a SELECT returns; it does not narrow which commands the policy applies to, and that is the gap.

A database-level control outside this repository — a BYPASSRLS revocation or a separate ownership model — could bound the owner-exemption half. No exported artifact accompanies the project, so per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN; the `for select` half is established from the macro alone and does not depend on it.

scope.established_by: Read the policy statement clause by clause against the grants issued by the companion macro on the same relations.

findings.title: Deleted customers are filtered out of the source dimension but never removed from the masked mart
findings.class: CWE-359 / retention: deletion does not propagate
findings.evidence: dim_customer.sql:42 excludes soft-deleted records with `where deleted_at is null`, and dim_customer.sql:30-40 does not carry `deleted_at` forward, so downstream models cannot see the flag. `customer_pii_masked` is incremental with `unique_key="customer_id"` (customer_pii_masked.sql:3-4), and its incremental predicate selects only rows whose `updated_at` has advanced (customer_pii_masked.sql:33). A dbt incremental merge inserts and updates matched keys; it issues no delete. A customer who disappears from `dim_customer` therefore simply stops being refreshed in the mart and their existing row remains.
findings.impact: Records for customers who have been deleted in the CRM persist indefinitely in the mart that every downstream consumer reads, and flow onward into the partner export through the join at partner_extract.sql:41-56. An erasure carried out at the source does not reach the analytics copy, and nothing in the project reports the divergence.
findings.recommendation: Carry `deleted_at` into `dim_customer` and handle deletions explicitly — a `delete+insert` incremental strategy keyed on the deleted set, or a post-hook that removes mart rows absent from the source. Add a dbt test asserting the mart has no `customer_id` missing from `dim_customer`, so the divergence fails a run rather than accumulating.

triage.reason: No compensating sweep exists: the project declares no snapshot, no delete post-hook and no retention job — dbt_project.yml's model config carries only schema, materialisation, hooks and grants.
The incremental path is the steady-state path for this model in every environment after its first build.
The retained rows are customer records; the full-rebuild branch makes them unmasked, and even masked they carry `display_name`, `billing_postcode` and the pseudonym.
The `unique_key` at customer_pii_masked.sql:4 narrows which rows are updated on a match; it does not cause absent rows to be removed.

scope.established_by: Followed a soft-deleted record through both models: excluded at the dimension, not represented in the mart's refresh predicate, retained by the merge semantics of the declared materialisation.

findings.title: The dbt development, CI and production targets read one identical credential triple, and the default target is development
findings.class: CWE-522 insufficiently protected credentials / absent environment separation
findings.evidence: All three targets interpolate the same three environment variables for host, user and password — profiles.yml:10-13, :22-25 and :34-37. profiles.yml:5 makes development the default target, and development and production share the same database name at :14 and :38. The development host default at :10 applies only when the variable is unset, so in any shell where the production variables are exported, a run with no explicit target connects to the production server with production credentials.
findings.impact: Which database is touched is decided by ambient environment rather than by the target name, and the target name is what a human reads before running a command. There is also no credential blast-radius boundary: one leaked value is simultaneously the development, CI and production credential, so a CI runner compromise is a production database compromise. The failure is quiet — the connection succeeds and models build into the development schema on the production server.
findings.recommendation: Give each target its own variable names so a target cannot silently borrow another environment's credentials, and issue distinct database roles per environment. Consider removing the default so the target must be named on every invocation.

triage.reason: For the exposed-secret reading only: no credential is in cleartext here — the user and password lookups are declared with no default and fail closed. That claim is ruled out separately; this finding is about credential scope, which FP-02 does not address.

The candidate narrowing is the per-target host default, but a default fires only when the variable is unset — in exactly the environment that has production credentials exported, it never fires — and the database name is identical for development and production.
No unskippable layer separates them: the TLS mode authenticates the server to the client and does nothing to stop a development-labelled run reaching the production server with the same credential.

A deployment injecting different values per environment under the same names would substantially bound this, and no CI, container or orchestration file exists anywhere under the target root. Caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all three output blocks key by key and compared the variable names and the database and schema pairs across them.
scope.narrowed_by: warehouse-dbt/profiles.yml:26 — the CI target uses a distinct database, so CI is separated; development and production are not.

findings.title: SessionStore.tokenFor accepts a host argument and ignores it
findings.class: CWE-1188 API that implies a control it does not implement
findings.evidence: SessionStore.kt:61-62 declares `fun tokenFor(host: String): String? = store().getString(KEY_TOKEN, null)`. The parameter is never read; the body is identical to `bearer()` on line 59. The doc comment above it reads 'Bearer to send to [host]', which states a per-host scoping the implementation does not perform. The one caller, AuthInterceptor.kt:23, is safe only because it performs the host comparison itself two lines earlier at AuthInterceptor.kt:19.
findings.impact: No exposure today — the single call site checks the host before calling. The defect is that the safety lives at the call site while the API signature advertises it, so a second caller written against the signature would send the token to any host and the code would read as correct.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the scoping — compare against the configured API host inside the function and return null otherwise — or delete the parameter and the comment so callers cannot mistake it for a control. Implementing it is preferable; it would also make the manual header in AttachmentUploader the only remaining unscoped path.

triage.reason: The real control is present on the only path that reaches this: AuthInterceptor.kt:19 returns early for any host other than `BuildConfig.API_HOST`. This is why the severity is low and the status is a hardening finding rather than an exposure.
It is retained rather than dropped because it is a latent trap whose cost is one new caller, and the tree already contains a caller that made exactly that mistake by hand (AttachmentSync.kt:80).

scope.established_by: Read the function body against its signature and comment, then enumerated its callers.
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-android/app/src/main/java/co/atlas/field/net/AuthInterceptor.kt:19 — the sole caller performs the host check itself.

findings.title: The certificate pin set carries an expiration date after which pinning stops being enforced
findings.class: CWE-324 use of a key past its expiration (MASVS-NETWORK-2)
findings.evidence: network_security_config.xml:14 sets `expiration="2027-03-01"` on the pin set for `api.fieldops.example`. Android's documented behaviour is to stop enforcing an expired pin set rather than to fail closed, so on that date platform pinning silently ceases while the configuration still reads as pinned. The OkHttp `CertificatePinner` duplicated at ApiClient.kt:23-26 does not expire and remains the effective control — which is a real compensating layer, but only in build variants that reach ApiClient.kt:44, and not for any traffic the platform layer alone would have covered.
findings.impact: On a fixed future date the platform-level protection lapses without any code change, build or alert, leaving a single remaining layer whose own applicability depends on a build flag. The failure is silent and dated, which is the property that makes it survive review.
findings.recommendation: Track the expiry as an operational deadline with an owner and rotate the pin set before it, or remove the attribute and manage pin rotation through releases. Either way, add a check that fails the build when the configured expiry is within one release cycle.

triage.reason: The duplicated OkHttp pinner at ApiClient.kt:23-26 and :44 has no expiry and enforces on the `api` client, which is why this is low rather than a loss of pinning. It does not fully exculpate: it is bypassed entirely when `ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS` is set, and it covers only hosts it enumerates.
The file is referenced from the application element at AndroidManifest.xml:13 and ships in every variant.

scope.established_by: Read the pin-set attributes and located the second, non-expiring pin implementation to establish what remains after the date.
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-android/app/src/main/java/co/atlas/field/net/ApiClient.kt:44 — the OkHttp pinner still applies on the api client in variants where insecure TLS is off.

findings.title: Three dependencies are declared and installed but imported nowhere
findings.class: CWE-1164 unnecessary installed attack surface
findings.evidence: The structured-logging package is declared at atlas-rag/pyproject.toml:12 and settlement-worker/pyproject.toml:11, and a search across the entire target root returns only those two manifest lines and no import — every module uses the standard library instead. The vector package is declared at atlas-rag/pyproject.toml:8 and appears only in a prose docstring; the vector is passed as a SQL cast at retriever.py:65, which needs the database extension rather than the Python package.
findings.impact: Three packages are resolved, downloaded and installed into both runtime environments with no code path to justify them. Each carries its own transitive tree and its own install-time execution surface, and each is a name an attacker can target in a confusion or squatting attack for no application benefit. It also misleads triage: a future advisory against the logging package would appear to affect two services that never call it.
findings.recommendation: Remove all three declarations. If structured logging is the intent, adopt it properly in one place; if not, drop it. Confirm the vector path needs no client-side adapter before removing it, since the SQL cast suggests it does not.

triage.reason: There is no sink reached at all — that is the finding, and a search across the full target root establishes it directly.
Checked the plausible benign reading, that the package is used indirectly: the adapter would require an explicit registration call, and a search for it returns nothing.
Bounded to low: an unused dependency is latent surface rather than an exploitable path today, becoming one only if the package is later compromised. Written down rather than dropped.

scope.established_by: Extracted every import statement from both packages, deduplicated, and set-differenced against the declared dependency lists; three declared names had no corresponding import.

findings.title: Document ACLs are enforced in Python after the database has returned the rows
findings.class: CWE-602 client-side enforcement of server-side security
findings.evidence: The SQL at retriever.py:63-70 filters on tenant and collection but not on `acl`; the column is selected at retriever.py:64 and the decision is made in the loop at retriever.py:79 by `_acl_allows`. The query asks for `k*3` rows (retriever.py:72) as a margin for the rows the loop will drop. So chunks the principal is not entitled to read are transferred from the database and held in the service process before being discarded.
findings.impact: Two consequences, neither catastrophic today. Content the caller may not see exists in process memory and would appear in a heap dump or a crash report. And the over-fetch factor is a fixed three: where more than two thirds of a tenant's nearest neighbours are ACL-denied, the caller silently receives fewer results than requested rather than the next eligible ones, which is a correctness failure that presents as poor retrieval quality.
findings.recommendation: Push the ACL into the query — an `acl && %(groups)s or '*' = any(acl)` predicate alongside the tenant clause — so the database never returns a row the principal cannot read and the limit applies to eligible rows.

triage.reason: The check does run before anything leaves the service: `_acl_allows` gates every append at retriever.py:79-81, and the resulting `hits` list is what reaches prompt assembly and the response. This is why the finding is low rather than an access-control bypass.
It is not merely a missing defence in depth: the over-fetch factor makes it a live correctness bug in retrieval completeness, so the finding is retained rather than dropped.
