scope.established_by: Compared the predicates present in the SQL with the predicates applied in Python for the same query.
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-rag/ragsvc/retriever.py:79 — the filter does execute before results are returned, which bounds this to a memory-exposure and completeness issue rather than a disclosure.

findings.title: The model gateway credential defaults to an empty string with no startup check
findings.class: CWE-1188 insecure default configuration
findings.evidence: settings.py:28 sets `model_api_key: str = os.getenv('MODEL_API_KEY', '')`. Its two readers construct clients with it unconditionally — app.py:87 and embedder.py:25 — and no code anywhere asserts it is non-empty; a grep for `model_api_key` returns the declaration and those two uses. Every other credential-shaped field in the file follows the same `os.getenv` pattern, so an unset variable is indistinguishable at runtime from a configured one until a request fails.
findings.impact: A deployment missing the variable starts normally and fails only when the first query reaches the gateway, turning a configuration error into a runtime outage rather than a startup failure. If the gateway at settings.py:27 accepts unauthenticated calls from inside the network, it fails open instead — the service would then call models with no attribution and no quota, and nothing in the tree establishes which of the two happens.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed at import: raise when `MODEL_API_KEY` is empty. A default that produces a silently misconfigured client is worse than a missing key that stops the process.

triage.reason: The finding is the absence of a credential, not the exposure of one; no secret value appears in the repository.

A deployment manifest that always injects the variable would bound this, and no such artifact exists anywhere under the target root. Per FP-08 absence of evidence is not HOLDS, which caps this at probable.

Bounded to low: the gateway is an internal host (settings.py:27) and the failure mode is most likely an error rather than an exposure. Written down because the fail-open direction cannot be excluded from this tree.

scope.established_by: Key-by-key enumeration of the Settings dataclass, then a reader census for the credential field.

findings.title: The playground credential is a compile-time constant with no environment override, so it cannot be rotated or disabled
findings.class: CWE-798 hardcoded credential with no rotation path
findings.evidence: settings.py:47 declares the value as a literal — the only field in the settings dataclass not read from the environment; every neighbour, including the model credential at settings.py:28, is. It authenticates: app.py:56 compares the presented bearer against it and returns a principal, reached from the request path at app.py:75 and from the token exchange at app.py:208.
findings.impact: The blast radius is genuinely bounded, and that is stated rather than inflated. What is not bounded is the operational property: because the value is a literal rather than an environment-backed field, the playground cannot be turned off and the key cannot be rotated without a code change, a rebuild and a redeploy. Any decision to retire the sandbox, or any need to respond to abuse of it, requires a release.
findings.recommendation: Read it from the environment with an empty default meaning the playground is disabled, matching the pattern of every other field in the same dataclass. That turns disabling the sandbox into a configuration change and gives the key a rotation path.

triage.reason: Not a template placeholder: it is compared against a live authorization header and returns a usable principal, so it functions as a real credential.

The exposure is intended and documented — settings.py:46 states the key is printed in the documentation and on the sandbox page, which the procedure names as an exculpation for a documented test-service key. Per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappearing, and it moves to the rotation gap reported here.

The scope is much narrower than a hardcoded credential normally implies: retriever.py:39-41 returns only the public collection for the demo tenant and retriever.py:56 forces the tenant into the query. The demo principal reaches the published FAQ and no other tenant's data, which is why the severity is low and the status is probable.
The data reachable with this key is the published FAQ collection, which is public content by definition.

scope.established_by: Symbol census for the field found the declaration and its single comparison site; the bounding path was traced through the collection resolver and the search function.
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-rag/ragsvc/retriever.py:39-41 and retriever.py:56 — the demo tenant is confined to the public collection and tenancy is forced server-side.

findings.title: The unauthenticated health endpoint discloses the environment name and internal cache size
findings.class: CWE-200 information exposure
findings.evidence: index.ts:18-20 answers `/healthz` with `{ ok, env: config.env, cache: cache.stats() }`. It is registered before the authentication middleware at index.ts:28 and is outside the `/api/v1` prefix that middleware covers, so it requires no credential. `cache.stats()` (cache.ts:37-39) returns the live entry count.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller learns the deployment environment and can watch the cache entry count change, which reveals write activity and the rough size of the tenant board over time. Neither is severe alone; the environment value is the more useful of the two because it tells an attacker whether the header-based identity path at auth.ts:59 is active.
findings.recommendation: Return only a liveness boolean on the unauthenticated endpoint and move the diagnostic fields behind authentication or onto a separate internal listener.

triage.reason: Real but bounded to a low-severity disclosure: no personal data, credential or record content is returned, only a configuration string and an integer. Severity is set accordingly and the finding is retained rather than deleted.
A health endpoint being publicly reachable is intended, but the two extra fields are not required for a liveness probe and are not bounded by that intent.

scope.established_by: Checked the route's position relative to the authentication middleware registration and read what each field in the response body resolves to.

findings.title: Rate-limit and cache maps grow without bound and are never swept
findings.class: CWE-401 / CWE-770 unbounded in-memory growth
findings.evidence: rateLimit.ts:8 declares a module-level `Map` that is written at rateLimit.ts:27 and rateLimit.ts:37 and never deleted from — an expired bucket is overwritten only if the same key returns, so a key seen once is retained for the process lifetime. cache.ts:5 has the same shape: entries are removed only on a subsequent read of the same key (cache.ts:19) or by `invalidateOrg` for that org prefix (cache.ts:30-34), so a cached page that is never requested again is retained indefinitely. Neither has a periodic sweep or a maximum size.
findings.impact: Steady memory growth proportional to the number of distinct client addresses and distinct org/status/page combinations ever seen, ending in an out-of-memory restart. It is slow and looks like a leak rather than an attack, which is why it survives.
findings.recommendation: Bound both structures — an LRU with a maximum entry count, or a periodic sweep that drops entries past their reset or expiry — and export the size as a metric so growth is visible before it is fatal.

triage.reason: Real but bounded: behind the load balancer the rate-limit key is a client address rather than a free-form header, so growth is proportional to distinct sources rather than to request count. Severity is set to low on that basis and the finding is still written down, as FP-10 requires.
The cache key includes `orgId` and `status` from the request (cache.ts:11, workorders.ts:53), so the key space is influenced by callers even though it is not arbitrary.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every write and every delete against both module-level maps; writes are unconditional, deletes are only on read-after-expiry or org invalidation.

findings.title: No audit logging anywhere in the stack, and the one logging control names a bucket the program never creates
findings.class: CWE-778 insufficient logging
findings.evidence: A search of the whole tree for flow logs, trail, bucket logging and distribution logging returns one hit: edge.ts:36, which enables access logs to a bucket name that no bucket resource in storage.ts declares. The VPC has no flow log, the three buckets have no access logging, the distribution has no logging configuration, and there is no trail and no alerting rule.
findings.impact: There is no record of who read the export or report objects, no flow record for the internet-facing database replica, and no request log for the reports distribution, so none of the exposures above would leave usable evidence. The single declared control names a bucket outside the program's state whose encryption, retention and public-access posture are unmanaged.
findings.recommendation: Declare the log bucket with the delivery policy, a lifecycle rule and all four block flags; add VPC flow logs, bucket access logging on the exports and reports buckets, and distribution logging. Send them to a destination with retention and an alert on permission change.

triage.reason: Logging may be centralised in a security account or enabled by a landing-zone policy, and the named bucket may exist out of band — but no exported artifact accompanies these files, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS. That caps the finding at probable.
It is not compensated elsewhere in the repository: the gap covers network, storage and edge alike.

scope.established_by: Inventoried every resource holding data or carrying a network path and diffed it against a tree-wide search for logging constructs.

findings.title: The production guard on deletion protection can never evaluate true
findings.class: CWE-670 always-incorrect control flow
findings.evidence: index.ts:39 builds a prefix combining the tenant slug and the environment, and index.ts:52-53 passes that prefix as the value edge.ts:31 compares against the literal production name. The compared value therefore always carries the tenant slug and never equals the literal, so no stack can satisfy it. It is the only such comparison in the tree.
findings.impact: The production load balancer can be deleted by any principal with the relevant permissions, including an errant destroy or a compromised deployment role, with no protection — and the code reads as though the protection is in place, so a reviewer will not look again. The same aliasing means any future environment guard added downstream is dead on arrival.
findings.recommendation: Pass the raw environment alongside the prefix and compare against that, or compute a boolean once in the entry point. Assert at startup that the environment config is one of a closed set.

triage.reason: The finding is about a guard that never evaluates true, not about an attacker-controlled value.
There is no narrowing elsewhere; edge.ts:31 is the whole condition and index.ts:53 is the only call site.
The control is not present in another layer: no other load balancer resource sets it and no stack policy is declared.

scope.established_by: Traced the parameter back to its single call site and its construction, and searched the tree for every comparison against the production name.

findings.title: Task-role trust policies carry no source-account or source-ARN confused-deputy condition
findings.class: CWE-284 service-principal trust without a source condition
findings.evidence: iam.ts:66-78 builds the same trust policy for all four services: a service principal, the assume action, and no condition block. The neighbouring partner role does carry conditions at iam.ts:101-104, so the omission is inconsistent within the same file.
findings.impact: The documented guardrail for service-principal trust — conditions scoping the role to this account and this cluster — is absent, so the roles are assumable by the service on behalf of any task definition it presents. It matters most for the role that currently holds unrestricted permissions.
findings.recommendation: Add source-account and source-ARN conditions to the trust policy built in the loop.

triage.reason: No service control policy or permissions boundary is declared that would restrict who may assume these roles.
The trust policy block contains no condition key at all, unlike the partner role in the same file.

Impact is bounded: the role can only be assumed by the service on behalf of a task definition, so exploitation needs an existing foothold. Severity is set to low on that basis and the finding is still written down.

scope.established_by: The trust policy is built once inside the loop, so it applies identically to all four roles.

findings.title: Second availability-zone subnet ranges fall outside the VPC range, so the network cannot converge
findings.class: CWE-1188 infrastructure declaration that cannot apply
findings.evidence: index.ts:41 creates the VPC with a /16 range. network.ts:49 and :61 compute each subnet's range from the loop index in a way that leaves the VPC range for the second zone, and the zone list at network.ts:18 has two entries. A subnet range outside its VPC range is rejected.
findings.impact: Only the first zone's subnets can be created, so the load balancer — which requires two zones — and both database subnet groups fail, leaving the stack partially applied with IAM roles and buckets present, including the world-readable exports bucket, while the network controls around them are not. A partial apply is also the state in which someone reaches for a manual console fix outside the code.
findings.recommendation: Derive the subnet blocks from the VPC range rather than from the loop index, and add a check that every subnet block is contained in it.

triage.reason: It is on the shipped path: the zone list is a module constant with two entries and the factory is called unconditionally.
There is no reading that makes the second zone's range a subset of the VPC range; the VPC range is a literal, not a variable that could widen.
No confidentiality or integrity impact of its own — the severity is low on that basis, and the finding stays written down because it changes how the rest of this report is read.

scope.established_by: Evaluated the range expression for each index of the zone constant against the VPC range literal.

findings.title: The reports bucket public access block leaves the two policy-related flags disabled
findings.class: CWE-668 incomplete public access block
findings.evidence: storage.ts:98-104 sets the two ACL-related flags true but leaves block-public-policy false at storage.ts:101 and restrict-public-buckets false at :103, on the bucket tagged as holding rendered customer reports.
findings.impact: Nothing prevents a policy with a wildcard principal from taking effect on the rendered customer reports bucket — from the console, from a future code change, or from a compromised deployment principal. The two flags that are set cover only ACLs, which is not the path a mistake would take.
findings.recommendation: Set all four flags true; the bucket is read through the distribution with an origin access control and by the partner role, neither of which needs a public policy.

triage.reason: No account or organisation control is declared in the tree, and the two flags that would provide the equivalent protection are precisely the ones disabled.
No public exposure is intended for this bucket, so there is nothing the disabled flags enable by design.
It is a preventive control that is simply absent; the finding stays as written, though the severity reflects that no public policy exists today.

scope.established_by: Read all four flags of every public access block in the tree individually.

findings.title: The linter is configured in both Python services with no rule selection, so no security rule runs
findings.class: CWE-1127 absent static analysis coverage
findings.evidence: settlement-worker/pyproject.toml:18-20 and atlas-rag/pyproject.toml:18-20 are the same three lines: the table header, a line length and a target version. There is no rule-selection key in either, so only the default rule set runs and the security family is not enabled in either project.
findings.impact: The lint gate is a formatting gate wearing a linter's name. It is not hypothetical: the hardcoded-credential rule targets exactly the constant at atlas-rag/ragsvc/settings.py:47, and the empty-secret default at settlement-worker/settlement/settings.py:38 is the shape the adjacent checks look for. Two of the defects in this report sit in files the configured linter reads on every run and cannot flag.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit rule selection including the security family to both manifests, with a per-file exception for test assertions once tests exist, and wire the check into a gate that fails the build.

triage.reason: Not a defence-in-depth nicety with a working equivalent elsewhere — no other static analysis is configured in either project. Kept at low because it is a missing detection control rather than an exploitable path.

A pipeline step invoking the linter with an explicit rule selection on the command line would override the config and bound this. No CI file exists anywhere under the target root, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and the finding is probable.
The construct is what it looks like: a valid, complete configuration selecting the defaults, and no separate linter configuration file exists in either project directory.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every table in both manifests; the linter table appears once in each with two keys and no rule sub-table.

findings.title: No test gate can run in any component, and one manifest points at a directory that does not exist
findings.class: CWE-1110 absent build-integrity gate
findings.evidence: settlement-worker/pyproject.toml:22-23 declares a test path, but the component directory contains only the manifest and the package — there is no tests directory, so the runner errors on a missing path rather than running anything. atlas-rag declares no test configuration at all. Neither package manifest declares a test script: fieldops-api/package.json:7-12 declares dev, build, start and typecheck, and pulumi-platform/package.json:6-10 declares preview, up and typecheck. warehouse-dbt/dbt_project.yml:8 sets a test path that exists and is empty.
findings.impact: Four components, four declared or implied quality gates, none of which executes a test. The manifest entry is the worst because it reads as configured coverage — a reviewer scanning it sees a test path and assumes tests run. No regression in signature verification, replay behaviour or credential handling would be caught by anything in this repository.
findings.recommendation: Either create the directory with real cases or remove the entry so the manifest stops advertising a gate that does not exist, and add a test script to both package manifests. Wire whatever is added to a pipeline, since with no CI in the tree even a correct script runs only when a human remembers.

triage.reason: The rule bounds a finding by showing a path does not ship; this finding is about an absent gate, not a shipped path.

Unusually for this class it can be answered from the tree: the missing directory is a fact about the repository, and no external control can supply a directory the runner resolves relative to the project root.
Real but not load-bearing on its own — it enables other defects to survive rather than being exploitable itself. Severity is held at low and the finding is still written down.

scope.established_by: Enumerated the scripts object of both package manifests and every table of both Python manifests, then listed each project directory to check whether the declared paths resolve.

findings.title: The journal insert interpolates the reference into the SQL string while binding its four neighbours
findings.class: CWE-89 SQL injection (defence-in-depth defect)
findings.evidence: ledger.py:78-83 binds four values as parameters and puts the fifth inside the statement by interpolation. The value is attacker-shaped — handlers.py:52, 61, 101 and 124 build it from the unvalidated message dict. It is not exploitable today: the reference pattern at schemas.py:16 is applied to the model field at schemas.py:43, every ledger entry in the tree is built through the validating constructor, and the pattern rejects every quote-bearing variant including trailing-newline forms.
findings.impact: None today. The defect is that a money-path SQL statement's safety rests entirely on one character class in another file, with no second control: widening the pattern to carry a memo or a partner reference — a one-line change that reads as harmless — turns this into injection against the audit journal with no other line changing.
findings.recommendation: Bind it like the other four values. There is no reason for the asymmetry.

triage.reason: schemas.py:16 constrains the value to an allowlisted character class before it reaches the sink and schemas.py:43 applies it to every construction path. This is why the finding ships as low and probable rather than as exploitable injection.
It is reported despite the exculpation because the pattern is a single point of failure with no defence behind it, and the correct construction is present two characters away in the same call.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all five execute sites; four bind every value, this one interpolates one. Traced the value back to its constraining pattern.
scope.narrowed_by: settlement-worker/settlement/schemas.py:16 — the reference pattern; the finding is the dependence on it, not a reachable injection.

findings.title: Reconciliation writes unvalidated partner-supplied fields into a line-oriented log
findings.class: CWE-117 improper output neutralization for logs
findings.evidence: The escaper tool flagged this as one of two uncleared calls out of ten. reconcile.py:70-72 logs the tenant and account, which arrive raw from the CSV reader at reconcile.py:45-46 — the patterns at schemas.py:14-15 are never applied on this path. A tenant value containing a carriage return and line feed followed by a plausible record forges log entries. The structured-logger exculpation does not apply: `structlog` is declared and imported nowhere, and the only configured formatter is line-oriented.
findings.impact: The adjustment log is what the finance team reads to review balance rewrites. Forged records hide a real adjustment among fabricated ones or attribute one to the wrong tenant.
findings.recommendation: Validate each CSV row against the existing models before use — which also fixes the balance-overwrite finding — or at minimum strip control characters. Emit one structured object per event so a newline cannot forge a record.

triage.reason: No pattern or allowlist runs between the CSV reader and the log call.
The sink is standard-library logging with the default line-oriented formatter.
The parameterised log style is not the exculpation; the finding is that no escaper reaches the sink, independent of how the string is built.
The loss is accountability over balance rewrites, which is the point of this particular log.

scope.established_by: Escaper tool over the component: ten logging calls in nine files, two uncleared; the other is a bound integer and is not reported.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires a malicious or tampered statement file, and the entry point has no caller in scope.

findings.title: The customer pseudonym is an unsalted digest keyed on a public version string
findings.class: CWE-916 weak hash for a low-entropy input / reversible pseudonymisation
findings.evidence: mask_pii.sql:33 computes `encode(digest(column || 'v3', 'sha256'), 'hex')`, where the appended value is `var("pii_policy_version")` — declared in cleartext as `pii_policy_version: v3` in dbt_project.yml:19. A single fast unsalted hash over a low-entropy identifier is enumerable: an attacker who knows the identifier space computes the whole mapping, and the version string is not a secret and does not vary per record. schema.yml:44-45 describes the result as a stable hash 'safe to join on across environments'.
findings.impact: The value provides no re-identification resistance, so any dataset it is exported in is as identifying as one carrying the raw identifier. It is not exposed today — `partner_extract` selects neither the pseudonym nor `customer_id` — but the field is documented as safe to share, which is the property that will put it in an export.
findings.recommendation: Use a keyed digest with a secret held outside the repository — `hmac(column, <secret>, 'sha256')` — and rotate the key rather than a public version string. Correct the column description, since 'safe to join on' is being read as 'safe to disclose'.

triage.reason: A reversible pseudonym of an identifier remains personal data; PRV-01 decides this, and the project treats `customer_id` as identifying throughout (schema.yml:24-25, 36-37).

Bounded to low: the pseudonym is not currently exported anywhere an adversary would receive it — partner_extract.sql:45-57 selects neither it nor customer_id — and the model that computes it already carries `customer_id` alongside (customer_pii_masked.sql:22), so today it adds no exposure. Written down because its documented purpose is to travel.
The salt substitute is a project variable in cleartext at dbt_project.yml:19, not a secret held outside the repository.

scope.established_by: Read the macro's expression and resolved its variable to the cleartext declaration, then checked every model that selects the resulting column.
scope.narrowed_by: warehouse-dbt/models/exports/partner_extract.sql:45 — the export does not currently select the pseudonym.
